entries.section: 1. A call to repentance:

paragraphs.text: 1 In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying, 2 “The LORD hath been sore displeased with your fathers. 3 Therefore say thou unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. 4 Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings: but they did not hear, nor hearken unto me, saith the LORD. 5 Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever? 6 But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers? and they returned and said, Like as the LORD of hosts thought to do unto us, according to our ways, and according to our doings, so hath he dealt with us.”

The prophet specified the date of his prophecy as the eighth month in the second year of Darius (520 B.C.), saying: “In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying” [1]. Here the prophet mentions his own name and the names of his father and his grandfather, perhaps mentioning his grandfather’s name because it was he who raised him after his father’s death, and because he was well known among those returning from the captivity (Neh 12:1, 4, 7).

entries.section: 1. A call to repentance:

paragraphs.text: The Lord’s call to them was: “The LORD hath been sore displeased with your fathers… Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts” [2-3]. We note here:

First: in this call He did not mention the details of their fathers’ past sins, for He did not want to wound their feelings after they had entered into the humiliation of captivity… Rather, even in urging them to repent, He wanted to support them, encourage them, and lift up their spirits.

Second: perhaps by their fathers He meant the generations before the captivity, which did not listen to the true prophets but followed the false prophets, so that the matter ended with the captivity of Israel and then of Judah. Or perhaps He meant those who had returned from the captivity about fifteen years earlier, who were negligent in building the temple and were absorbed in their earthly pleasures (Hag 1). These, in their zeal, had returned from the captivity to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, but since they did not return to the Lord with their hearts, the work stopped and they lost their spiritual life. Therefore the Lord affirms: “Turn ye unto me… and I will turn unto you.” Before the return to the place, He asks for the return of the heart to Him, while for His part He is ready, indeed longing, to return to us and build His spiritual temple within us. This is God’s continual call to us, and as St. Augustine says: [God in His long-suffering waits for the sinner, saying: “Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you.”] He also says: [By our complete return to God we find Him ready, as the prophet says: “We shall find Him ready as the morning” (Hos 6:3, Septuagint). God is not absent; He is present in every place, and it is we who lose Him by our deviation, for it is said: “He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not” (Jn 1:10). He was in the world and the world did not know Him, because the impurity of our eyes keeps us from seeing Him.] He also says: [God has forsaken you because you are the one who forsook. You are the one who fell away from Him, but as for Him, He does not fall away from you…].

Thus returning to God is not merely a change of place, that is, leaving Babylon and going to Jerusalem, but a change in the soul’s position toward God: instead of turning its back to Him with its evil deeds, it gives Him its face, drawing near to Him spiritually. As St. Didymus the Blind says: [This separation and this approach must not be understood as taking place in a particular place, but through the attitude and disposition of the spirit].

entries.section: 1. A call to repentance:

paragraphs.text: Third: He asks them to take warning from what happened to their fathers: “Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?” [5]. Perhaps He meant that He had forewarned their fathers through the prophets, but only for a time, and since they rejected the warning, they perished and lost the prophets. St. Didymus the Blind sees that He means by the prophets here the false prophets who deceived their fathers by saying to them: “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 11:8). They perished together with the false prophets who deceived them, and so the deceivers disappeared together with those who let themselves be deceived by their lies.

Fourth: in His call to return, God is called “the LORD of hosts,” His name being repeated three times in one passage [3]. On the one hand, the Lord comes forward to them as the Lord of hosts, to declare His responsibility for the work, so that they should not fear those who oppose, for He is able to accomplish the work through them if they submit to Him as spiritual soldiers to their commander. As for the expression “the LORD of hosts” three times at His call to repentance, it is an affirmation of the work of the Holy Trinity in their lives, for man cannot return to God unless he experiences the self-giving love of the Father, the grace of the Son through the Cross, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, the giver of forgiveness.

entries.section: 1. A call to repentance:

paragraphs.text: Fifth: this book affirms the important principle that God had already declared in the books of the prophets before the captivity, that what befalls them is chastening from the Lord, yet at the same time it is nothing but the natural fruit of sin… “According to our ways, and according to our doings, so hath he dealt with us” [6]. It is man himself who casts himself under chastening as the fruit of his deeds.

Sixth: if their fathers perished because of their clinging to evil, then whoever clings to vanity becomes vain; the remedy is to cling to the truth that he may live eternally. Thus God presents His word, that is, the truth, that we may cling to it and not die… “But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers?” [6]. As Isaiah says: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

entries.section: 2. The vision of the horses:

paragraphs.text: 7 Upon the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Sebat, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying, 8 I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white. 9 Then said I, O my lord, what are these? And the angel that talked with me said unto me, I will shew thee what these be. 10 And the man that stood among the myrtle trees answered and said, These are they whom the LORD hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth. 11 And they answered the angel of the LORD that stood among the myrtle trees, and said, We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest.

entries.section: 2. The vision of the horses:

paragraphs.text: Three months after the beginning of his prophecy came the month of Shebat, in which the trees put forth their shoots and the sweet fragrance of the myrtle tree spreads. Perhaps the prophet used to spend the whole day in a valley near him, falling on his knees under the shade of the myrtle trees, his tears never drying, crying out: “O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years?” [12]. In the midst of his weeping he turned his heart toward the temple which had become a ruin, and toward the people who had come about fifteen years earlier to build the temple, but each one was absorbed in his own work and personal interests. The prophet, as a priest, was groaning, longing for the return of the temple with its spiritual rites, which he had not practiced from his birth until that moment. Therefore at night God granted him this vision: “I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white. Then said I, O my lord, what are these? And the angel that talked with me said unto me, I will shew thee what these be. And the man that stood among the myrtle trees answered and said, These are they whom the LORD hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth. And they answered the angel of the LORD that stood among the myrtle trees, and said, We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest” [8-11].

By this vision God declares His saving plans and His care for His spiritual house. God also gave him an angel to speak with him, who accompanied him in all the visions, entering into dialogue with him and explaining to him what was obscure to him. It is as though the Lord wanted to affirm heaven’s support for him and the ministry of the angels to men (Heb 1:14).
Now, who is this man riding on a red horse, standing among the myrtle trees that were in the shade, who is called “the angel of the LORD”?

The expression “the angel of the LORD” most often refers to God Himself when He appears as an angel or a messenger for the sake of man, for the word “angel” means “messenger.” It is stated in the Babylonian Talmud: “This man is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He, for it is said: ‘The LORD is a man of war.’” St. Didymus the Blind says: [The one riding on a red horse is the Lord the Savior incarnate, and the red horse is the body that He put on. The prophet saw Him “standing among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom,” that is, among the shaded mountains. The mountains are the two Testaments. They are for me fertile mountains, shaded because of the wealth of thoughts and the abundance of the texts of Scripture about the Incarnate One].”

We can say that the prophet saw this vision “by night” [8], that is, during the Old Testament, when the Lord Christ, the Sun of Righteousness who turned the night of the world into day, had not yet appeared. He saw Him through the prophecies, therefore he saw Him in the shade, His coming not yet having been fulfilled. He saw Him as a man riding upon a red horse, since He became incarnate and became man, coming forward to us with His divine work through the Cross, where the blood was shed, as Isaiah said: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments… Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat? I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” (Isa 63:1-3).

The prophet saw behind the Lord Christ red, speckled, and white horses, of whom the Lord said: “These are they whom the LORD hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth” [10]. With the coming of the Lord Christ to us for salvation, heaven was opened and the heavenly ones turned to the service of man on behalf of the heavenly Bridegroom, and became like those who walk to and fro through the earth to minister to those who shall be heirs of salvation (Heb 1:14).

Perhaps those whom the Lord sent to walk to and fro through the earth are the men of the Old Testament who prepared the earth to receive the Incarnate Word through their teachings and prophecies; these preceded Him on the way, yet they remain behind Him as their Lord and Savior. As for their answer: “We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest” [11], it points to the preparation of the earth to receive the Messiah the Savior, for the way had been prepared and the time was suitable for His coming down.

If the rider on the red horse symbolizes the Incarnate Word of God, then these horses of different colors perhaps signify the divine works, as though the prophet is declaring to the Jewish people at that time that God had offered various works and prepared for them by every means an atmosphere of calm: the whole earth is still and at rest, there is no one to oppose and no one to devise plots against them, so they must hasten to build the house of the Lord. In the same sense we say that the prophet declares that the Lord Christ has sent us His red, speckled, and white horses, offering us every heavenly gift and divine bestowal in order to make our earth, that is, our body, still and calm, not resisting the Spirit but working with Him for the glory of God. It is a time for work, in which it is fitting for us to consecrate all our spiritual and bodily energies to the spiritual building of our heavenly Jerusalem.

This is the first vision that lifted Zechariah out of his daily tears in the valley of the myrtle trees under the shade, to bring him into the valley of the work of God declared through the Incarnation and the crucifixion! By this Zechariah was taken from the distress of his soul to true peace and rest, therefore he said: “All the earth sitteth still, and is at rest.”

Let us not understand the earth’s being at rest and still in the sense of idleness and slackness, but in the sense of enjoying the surpassing peace of God, as St. Didymus the Blind says: [The rational soul carries an energy that moves it in continual activity, but since it works for the sake of the good, it remains calm and at rest without disturbance, enjoying the inner peace that the fear of God brings… As it is written: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil” (Prov 1:33)].

In Christ Jesus our Lord our souls and also our bodies, that is, our inner heavens and our earth, become at rest, being sanctified by Him and rejoicing, though bearing His cross and entering with Him into His tomb.

entries.section: 3. The Lord’s jealousy for His house:

paragraphs.text: 12 Then the angel of the LORD answered and said, O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years? 13 And the LORD answered the angel that talked with me with good words and comfortable words. 14 So the angel that communed with me said unto me, Cry thou, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy. 15 And I am very sore displeased with the heathen that are at ease: for I was but a little displeased, and they helped forward the affliction. 16 Therefore thus saith the LORD; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem. 17 Cry yet, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; My cities through prosperity shall yet be spread abroad; and the LORD shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem.

entries.section: 3. The Lord’s jealousy for His house:

paragraphs.text: If the prophet Zechariah spent years contemplating the ruin of the temple with tears that never dried, asking God for the rebuilding of the temple, then our Lord Jesus Christ is the only propitiatory Intercessor who cries out with His precious blood for the raising up of His sanctuaries in humanity, for it is said: “Then the angel of the LORD answered and said, O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years?” Humanity fell under the captivity of the enemy of good for years of such measure, and no one could intercede for it except the One who offered His blood as an atonement for our sins, bringing divine mercy by paying the debt of divine justice on the Cross. His intercession was not mere words but a work full of love and effective, by which He was able to remove the divine wrath from those who believe in Him and bring them into God’s mercies, that His holy heavenly temple might be raised up in them. This is the good words and comfortable words which the angel who accompanied him declared [13].

entries.section: 3. The Lord’s jealousy for His house:

paragraphs.text: By the Cross the Lord says: “I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy. And I am very sore displeased with the heathen that are at ease: for I was but a little displeased, and they helped forward the affliction. Therefore thus saith the LORD; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem. Cry yet, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; My cities through prosperity shall yet be spread abroad; and the LORD shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem” [14-17]. From the historical side this was fulfilled literally: after the captivity of Judah for seventy years God declared His jealousy for His city and His people, when the nations were at ease, thinking that they had completely humbled the people of God, laid waste the Promised Land, and destroyed the holy temple; some of them took the main part, like the Babylonians, and others shared in the work, like the Edomites, or by gloating… But while they were at ease the Lord returned to Jerusalem to raise up His house anew and to permit the stretching forth of the line (the instrument for measuring the wall), not for demolition as at the time of the captivity because of the crookedness of the walls, but for the raising of buildings and rebuilding; and thus He pours out good upon His people and declares His love and care for them.

This was fulfilled literally in the sixth century B.C., but it was fulfilled in a fuller way and with a deeper meaning in the Messianic age, when the Lord ascended His Cross stretching out His hands with blessing to humanity, shattering the captivity of the devil and granting true good to those who believe in Him, as St. Paul says: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Rom 8:32). He returned to us with His mercies to raise up His temple in us, saying: “The kingdom of God is within you.” He stretched forth His hand with the line to build and increase our inner life, so that blessings and consolations overflow from the fruit of His Holy Spirit (Jn 15:26), revealing His choice of our inner Jerusalem as His bride.
What is this house that occupies the heart of God?

First: the Church which the Lord raises up as His bride, to which the Apostle pointed by his saying: “But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Tim 3:15).

Second: St. Didymus says: [This house is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose heart is a dwelling for Him, one with the divinity without mixing or separation, of which He said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… But he spake of the temple of his body” (Jn 2:19, 21). This is the house announced by the book of Proverbs: “Wisdom hath builded her house” (Prov 9:1)].

Third: St. Didymus concludes his discourse on this house by saying: [We must also add that every believer is likewise a house built to be a temple of God. Scripture says: “Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” (1 Cor 3:16). The Savior Himself says plainly: “If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him” (Jn 14:23)].

entries.section: 4. The vision of the four horns:

paragraphs.text: 18 Then lifted I up mine eyes, and saw, and behold four horns. 19 And I said unto the angel that talked with me, What be these? And he answered me, These are the horns which have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. 20 And the LORD shewed me four carpenters. 21 Then said I, What come these to do? And he spake, saying, These are the horns which have scattered Judah, so that no man did lift up his head: but these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah to scatter it.

entries.section: 4. The vision of the four horns:

paragraphs.text: According to the Hebrew canon, the second chapter of this book begins with this second vision, concerning the appearance of the four horns which scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem so that no man did lift up his head [21], and then the appearance of four craftsmen who rose up to spread terror and to cast out these horns of the Gentiles.

Perhaps the prophet Zechariah in his solitude was looking in every direction of the inhabited world, to see the nations as though they were striking Jerusalem with their horn without ceasing and without mercy. The Jews were familiar with the tending of sheep and knew the blows of the horns of horned beasts, how they kill the sheep and scatter them; therefore the psalmist says: “Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps 22:21). The prophet Daniel speaks of the horn that made war with the saints and prevailed against them until the Ancient of days came (Dan 7:21-22). Thus horns became a sign of power and authority, for the Lord says in Micah: “Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the LORD, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth” (Mic 4:13).
In this vision of the four horns the following is to be noted:

First: some see in these four horns a reference to the kingdoms that humbled the people, namely the kingdom of Assyria and Babylon, the kingdom of the Medes and the Persians, the kingdom of the Chaldeans, and the kingdom of the Romans. God sent to each kingdom a craftsman to scatter it and humble it, and behold, the four kingdoms have completely vanished, their horns having been shattered, while the work of God remains successful, as the psalmist says: “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed… He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision” (Ps 2). These kingdoms were indicated by the four metals and the four great beasts which came up from the sea, one after another, in the vision of the prophet Daniel.

Second: Origen, St. Augustine, and many of the Fathers of the Church see that the number 4 refers to the four quarters of the world, that is, to the love of the world, and also refers to the body as being of the dust of this world. It is as though these horns that scatter “Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem” [19], “so that no man did lift up his head” [21], mean that the love of the world and the lusts of the body shatter Judah, that is, our union with the Lord Christ who came forth from the tribe of Judah, and shatter the new Israel, that is, our inner membership and the purity of our heart by which we see God. By them man does not lift up his head, but bows down his soul to be buried in the dust, as happened with the one who had the one talent (Mt 25:18); instead of rising with his body to heaven, his soul with the lusts of his body bows down to the earth.

Third: as Satan stirred up four horns against Jerusalem, God sent four craftsmen, as though God supports His children according to the extent that they enter into trials or afflictions; the more intense the warfare of Satan, the more help He sends. This is the work of God throughout the ages: since Pharaoh was violent, God sent Moses; since Ahab was wicked, God sent Elijah; and when Arius rose up against the Church, God prepared Athanasius the Apostolic; and so on. What goes on at the level of the Church of the Old Testament or of the New Testament is fulfilled every day in the life of each one of us.

Fourth: some of the Fathers see that the four horns are the warfare of the devil from every side, of which the Apostle Paul speaks: “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places” (Eph 6:12), and the Church has needed the four Gospels as the craftsmen who spoil the work of the devil with his four horns. Indeed Satan has used violent warfare with his four horns, but the Gospels have presented to us a new craft for overcoming Satan, which is the way of love and meekness; for the fire of the devil, with which he inflames the hearts of men against the believer, is overcome by love. As St. John Chrysostom says, fire is not put out by fire but by water; thus evil is not resisted by evil but by good.

And it is marvelous that, despite the meekness that characterized the four craftsmen, the horns trembled before them, just as Herod, the man of authority, feared before the unarmed St. John the Baptist (Mk 6:20), and as Felix the governor trembled before St. Paul the prisoner standing before him for trial (Acts 24:25)!

entries.section: 1. The measuring of Jerusalem and its glory:

paragraphs.text: 1 I lifted up mine eyes again, and looked, and behold a man with a measuring line in his hand. 2 Then said I, “Whither goest thou?” And he said unto me, “To measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof, and what is the length thereof.” 3 And, behold, the angel that talked with me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him, 4 and said unto him, “Run, speak to this young man, saying, Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein: 5 for I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her.

The Lord Christ Himself comes forward as a man with a measuring line in His hand to build His house in us by His Holy Spirit, that it may correspond to His heavenly house which St. John saw, the heavenly Jerusalem (Rev 11:1-2; 21:15; etc.).

The prophet says, “I lifted up mine eyes and looked,” repeating this phrase in more than one place (Zech 1:18; 2:1; 5:1; 6:1). Since this book proclaims the evangelical thought concerning the salvation of the world, it would not have been possible for the prophet Zechariah to grasp it unless God lifted up his inner eyes by the spirit of prophecy to see and understand God’s thought toward man. I say it is a call directed to all of us to lift up our eyes by the Holy Spirit, so that our understanding may not stop at the limits of the letter but enter into the hidden mysteries of God and look upon His saving works, things that cannot be experienced with eyes blinded in the dust of this world.

He saw “a man with a measuring line in his hand” [1]. Perhaps this man is the Word of God, who for our sake became man. He is the one whom he had seen before riding upon a red horse, standing among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom (Zech 1:8), who has come to plan the buildings of His holy Church. St. Didymus the Blind says: [He is the Lord the Savior to whom the prophet Zechariah points by his saying: “Behold the man whose name is The Branch; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD” (Zech 6:12, Septuagint). He is the true light of whom John the Baptist speaks: “This was he of whom I spake, He that cometh after me is preferred before me: for he was before me” (Jn 1:15). He is the builder of Jerusalem, who drew the foundation and laid it as an architect. Since Jerusalem was torn down by the enemies who besieged it, He measures its length and breadth in order to lay the foundations upon which the walls are raised in the proper places, with order and arrangement. St. Paul the Apostle writes of this city for which all who pleased the Lord by their faith were waiting: “which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 10:11). The prophet Ezekiel also says: “and, behold, there was a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass, with a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate” (Ezek 40:3)].

In the book of Revelation we see the holy temple and the altar measured with a rod, while the outer court is cast out and not measured (Rev 11:1-2), as though our Lord Jesus wants to reassure us that the true children of God who have been sanctified to Him are kept and known to Him, while those who are outside the faith are outside the measure, not worthy to be the subject of His knowledge… Therefore He rebukes them saying: “I know you not whence ye are” (Lk 13:27).
As for the measuring reed, it is of gold (Rev 21:15), that is, heavenly, because spiritual and heavenly things are measured only by what is spiritual.

entries.section: 1. The measuring of Jerusalem and its glory:

paragraphs.text: What is the measuring line or spiritual measuring reed held by our Architect for the raising up of the holy Jerusalem but the holy Cross, which is made of two beams, one lengthwise and one crosswise? By this Cross He defines the dimensions of His holy city in us, saying: “To measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof, and what is the length thereof” [2]. On the crosswise beam of the wood of the Cross the Lord Christ stretched out His hands to gather with the one the Jews and with the other the Gentiles, that all together might be one in Him. As St. Irenaeus says: [He who gathers all things in Himself was hanged on the tree]. And Pope Athanasius: [It was fitting for the Lord to stretch out His hands… that with the one He might gather the ancient people and with the other the Gentiles, and unite them together in Himself]. This is the breadth of the new Jerusalem, for it is fitting for the believer to bear the mark of his crucified Savior, stretching out his hands in love to embrace all humanity in his heart as his brethren. As for the lengthwise wood, upon it the body of the Lord was nailed, lifted up above the earth, fulfilling His promise: “And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me” (Jn 12:32), accomplishing reconciliation between the Father and man in His crucified body. As St. Hippolytus says: [The Cross is Jacob’s ladder; this tree with heavenly dimensions rose from the earth to heaven, setting itself up as an eternal planting between heaven and earth, that it might lift up the whole world]. This is the length of the new Jerusalem, where it is fitting for us to be nailed with Him on the wood, to accept the opening of heaven upon earth and the rising of earth to heaven. It is as though the dimensions of our new Jerusalem are, in its breadth, the widening of our heart to every person, and its length is its opening to heaven; in other words, it is the practice of the commandment of love in Christ Jesus our Lord, a love for all humanity in the heavenly God.

entries.section: 1. The measuring of Jerusalem and its glory:

paragraphs.text: The prophet Zechariah continues his discourse by saying: “And, behold, the angel that talked with me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him, and said unto him, Run, speak to this young man, saying, Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein: for I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her” [4-5].
What a vision that gladdens the heart, for it reveals the work of God with us!

First: His sending of the angels, for one angel goes forth and another behind him, and the subject of their discourse is our Jerusalem, the dwelling of God with men. In the book of Revelation we see the angels in continual movement, declaring their longing for the last day or the harvest (Rev 14:15-20), longing to see the bride crowned with glory together with her Bridegroom.

Perhaps the first angel refers to the heavenly ones who waited for the fulfillment of the prophecies to rejoice at the salvation of man and his return to communion with them in their liturgies and praises of God, while the second angel refers to them as they went forth in the New Testament rejoicing at the fulfillment of what they had long awaited.

Second: most likely by the young man here [4] is meant the prophet Zechariah or the believer in general. For if the Lord Christ shared in humanity, becoming an embryo, then a child, a boy, a youth, and a man, yet He did not become an old man according to the body, so that His bride may always remain in a spiritually renewed youth, without the old age of helplessness and weakness, and each member of her sings, saying: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor 4:16), “But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isa 40:31), “thy youth is renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps 103:5).

St. Didymus the Blind says: [The holy man is a young man in the sight of God’s angels, especially when he puts on the new man, and then it can be said of him: “Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right” (Prov 20:11)… And John the Apostle says in his epistle about those who advance in virtue: “I have written unto you, young men, because ye are strong, and the word of God abideth in you, and ye have overcome the wicked one” (1 Jn 2:14). So whoever is young in the Spirit receives the teachings of the angel who goes forth to reveal to him the revelations that we see in the rest of the prophecy.”

Third: He reveals to us the dimensions of the new Church, saying: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men and cattle therein.” She becomes like open country not bounded by a material wall because of its being crowded with men and cattle, for she is the city of love without limits. The soul carries within it the Kingdom of God, widened by love for all, with a glorious inner joy. As for her being crowded with men and cattle, it refers to the sanctification of the soul with unlimited energies and the sanctification of the body, which was animal, with new possibilities without limit. It is as though our inner Jerusalem has room for every person, through the sanctification of soul and body together with all their possibilities and gifts.

entries.section: 1. The measuring of Jerusalem and its glory:

paragraphs.text: Fourth: if our inner Jerusalem is like open country not bounded by material walls, yet it has a unique wall. “For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about” [5]. This is the wall of fire which the Only-Begotten Son sent to us from the Father after His ascension, when it came upon the disciples in the form of tongues of fire on the day of Pentecost, to surround the Church on every side, to keep her from every evil dart, and to kindle her with the continual warmth of the Spirit. Therefore the believer sings: “By my God have I leaped over a wall” (Ps 18:29), “The LORD is the strength of my life” (Ps 27:1), and as St. Jerome says: [The enemies have besieged me; thou art therefore my fortress.] The enemies have aimed their fiery arrows at my heart, but the divine fire surrounds me as a wall to devour the fire of evil and consume it, as the rod of Moses, which became a serpent, devoured the serpents of the magicians! Thus instead of the deadly fire of evil, he is kindled with the holy divine fire.
God is a wall of fire around us, kindling our heart with the fire of love, so that we do not become like those of whom it was said: “the love of many shall wax cold” (Mt 24:12).

Thus by this divine wall the enemy has no hope against us, saying: “I will go up to the land of unwalled villages; I will go to them that are at rest, that dwell safely, all of them dwelling without walls, and having neither bars nor gates, to take a spoil, and to take a prey…” (Ezek 38:11-12).

Fifth: the Lord says, “and will be the glory in the midst of her” [5]. If the Lord Christ is the pearl of great price which we possess within us, then by His divine fires surrounding us no one is able to gaze upon this pearl shining within us because of its surpassing beauty and its radiance that cannot be looked upon. His splendor becomes our splendor, and His glory is on our account, saying to us as to His bride: “and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom. And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezek 16:13-14).

entries.section: 2. Her flight from Babylon:

paragraphs.text: 6 Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north, saith the LORD: for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heaven, saith the LORD. 7 Deliver thyself, O Zion, that dwellest with the daughter of Babylon. 8 For thus saith the LORD of hosts; After the glory hath he sent me unto the nations which spoiled you: for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye. 9 For, behold, I will shake mine hand upon them, and they shall be a spoil to their servants: and ye shall know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me.

If God Himself has measured the city and surrounded it by His Holy Spirit as a wall of fire and has been revealed in its midst with His glory, all this urges it the more to strive, fleeing from every stumbling block, lest it lose the work of God in it. Therefore He calls to it: “Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north” [6].

From the literal historical side, it is a divine call to those who clung to the land of captivity because of their private interests; therefore He calls them to flee from Babylon, “the land of the north,” to the Promised Land; and here He mentions no name or title for them, because by their clinging to a humiliating life they became unworthy of the knowledge of God, and are called “Ho, ho,” like those who are unknown! But from the spiritual side the call is standing and continuing through the ages for every person. As for His repeating the particle of address “Ho,” it is because the call is directed to the Jews as to the Gentiles, that they leave the land of satanic captivity where the cold north wind blows (Sir 43:20), quenching the flame of love in the heart, and go not to another land but to heaven itself, through the fires of the Holy Spirit who lifts it from the land of the north and goes with it from glory to glory to bring it into the bosom of the Father in Christ Jesus our Lord! It is a repeated call that includes the rich as well as the poor, the man as well as the woman, to leave the land of evil with its dust and its mire and return by the Holy Spirit to the divine sanctuaries. This call, as St. Didymus the Blind says, means: [“Flee from evil,” “Depart from evil, and do good” (Ps 34:14), and also: “Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil” (Isa 1:16)]. This is accomplished by our abstaining from every kind of evil and holding fast to what is praiseworthy, as the Apostle Paul commands: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil” (1 Thess 5:21-22). For whoever looks to the good, desiring it and fulfilling it, flees from evil.

If God permitted their being scattered as the four winds of heaven because of their evil, He calls them to leave their places and go forth to Zion to enjoy deliverance (salvation), saying: “for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heaven, saith the LORD. Deliver thyself, O Zion, that dwellest with the daughter of Babylon” [6-7]. We note in His discourse here the following:

First: God wants us to go forth from Babylon, which means confusion and disturbance, to enter Zion, where there is inner peace and a life of joy and praise. St. Didymus says: [The place of salvation is holy Zion, in which those who formerly dwelt with the daughter of Babylon can be saved… And as the name “Babylon” means confusion, everyone whose spirit is troubled is a Babylonian; therefore we must be delivered from this state if we desire to return to Zion; then we shall sing praises and strike the harps in honor of God, for there it is fitting for us to chant to God and play for Him, as it is written: “Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Zion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed” (Ps 65:1), and also: “Sing praises to the LORD, which dwelleth in Zion: declare among the people his doings” (Ps 9:11). It is impossible for us to praise God and play for Him while we dwell with the daughter of Babylon in the north; therefore the Holy Spirit cries with a full voice: Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north, saith the LORD, that you may take refuge in Zion, O dwellers with the daughter of Babylon, for I gather you from the four winds, that is, from the ends of all the earth].

Therefore let us flee from the confusion of sin and take refuge in the peace of Zion, where there is the divine fortress, so that the soul may be lifted up to be found in the righteousness of God, enjoying the peace of truth. As St. Jerome says: [As long as we are in the state of grace our soul is at peace, but when we begin to play with sin our soul becomes troubled like a boat battered by the waves].

Second: what are the four winds that God permitted to scatter them from Jerusalem but the evil spirits whom God permits to be left to chasten the one who delivers himself to them by his own will? We need not wonder at this, for the Apostle Paul judged the young man who sinned with his father’s wife “to deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor 5:5). For although the love of God protects us from the power of the wicked one, His providence sometimes permits our being delivered to the bitterness of this enemy to whom we ourselves delivered ourselves, accepting him as our father instead of God our Father (Jn 8:44); then we realize in bitterness our need of the true fatherhood of God.

Perhaps by the winds are meant here the strange teachings that shake the soul to break it, which could not affect St. John the Baptist, for the Lord Christ says of him: “What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken with the wind?” (Mt 11:7). As St. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, comments: [Did you go out to see a man empty of the knowledge of God, who responds to the breezes of every unclean spirit?] And as St. Augustine comments: [Surely John was not a reed shaken by the wind, for he was not carried about by every wind of doctrine]. And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [The (four winds) may be the different currents of teachings, which make those who walk improperly in thought have evil thoughts and vain works, swaying here and there. The Apostle Paul says: “That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive” (Eph 4:14)].
Perhaps by the four winds are meant the trials and afflictions that sweep away and shatter souls built upon the sand and not upon the rock.

Perhaps also the four winds refer to the love of the world and the lusts of the body that shake the soul, for we saw that the number (4) refers to these things in our interpretation of the four horns.

Third: it is not enough to flee from Babylon; we must flee to Zion, meaning that it is not enough to flee from the confusion of evil, but it is fitting for us to take refuge (Zion) in the righteousness of Christ our Lord. In the positive side of the work St. Paul says: “But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel” (Heb 12:22-24). Thus our Lord Jesus by His blood takes us out of evil to bring us into Zion, that we may live on a heavenly level.

entries.section: 2. Her flight from Babylon:

paragraphs.text: Finally, since the Lord brings us back from our satanic captivity and brings us into His divine Kingdom, He returns to punish the devil who humbled us, saying: “After the glory hath he sent me unto the nations which spoiled you: for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye. For, behold, I will shake mine hand upon them, and they shall be a spoil to their servants: and ye shall know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me” [8-9].
In our study of some of the books of the prophets we noticed that God, who uses the nations for chastening, when the nations become puffed up against His people returns and punishes these nations.

Here He says “after the glory”; perhaps He meant after the Cross, where man was brought back from captivity and God was glorified in him, and at the same time He repaid the devil for his evil by shattering his authority. The enemy who humbled the children of God and spoiled them has become, in Christ Jesus, under humiliation, with no authority over them (Col 2:14-15).

What does “toucheth the apple of his eye” mean? The devil, who stretched out his hand to us and made us lose our spiritual sight, has his work rebound upon him, so that his blindness increases day by day, as though by his increasing evil he touches the apple of his own eye until the cup of his blindness is full! And what we say of the devil we say of man: by doing evil to his brother he touches the apple of his own eye and loses spiritual sight, as though, while he is harming his brother’s body or possessions or reputation, he is aiming his blows at his own inner eyes.

Evil does not rebound only into the loss of inner sight but also touches his whole being, by the Lord’s saying: “they shall be a spoil to their servants,” for while he thinks that he is shattering his brethren, his servants plunder him. Who are these servants but the senses and emotions of the body, which become uncontrolled because of his evil, so that they rob him of every blessing in him? This is what we observe in practice: when we rage against our brethren, the lusts of the body rage within us and we lose all chastity and self-control, because by our raging against our brethren we lose our mastery over our depths, and the grace of God, the giver of chastity and purity, withdraws!

entries.section: 3. Jerusalem and the Incarnation:

paragraphs.text: 10 Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for, lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the LORD. 11 And many nations shall be joined to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people: and I will dwell in the midst of thee, and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto thee. 12 And the LORD shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land, and shall choose Jerusalem again. 13 Be silent, O all flesh, before the LORD: for he is raised up out of his holy habitation.

If this vision fills the soul with joy, in which the Lord Christ appears as a man with a measuring line in His hand to measure in us His new heavenly Jerusalem, then the secret of true joy is His dwelling in her, for He says: “Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for, lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, saith the LORD” [10]. Fr. John of Kronstadt says: [The mark of sin is disturbance and gloom, while the mark of the righteousness of Christ is inner peace and joy. Thus the Jews hung their harps upon the willows in the land of captivity, for gloom filled their lives, saying: “How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a strange land?” (Ps 136). And by their return to Zion joy returned to them and their lives were turned into praise. St. Didymus the Blind says: [As in the time of the captivity there was lamentation and groaning among the Hebrews because the Lord had departed from the offenders, so at their return to the spiritual mother called Zion He gives them a command to sing and rejoice (sing and rejoice), because the Lord has come and dwelt in her midst, for the temple has indeed been raised up and God has made it His dwelling… The saved captives enjoy this security, saying: “When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing” (Ps 126:1-2)… They were groaning when they were scattered from their homeland in the bonds of captivity, so it is natural that they exult and rejoice when they return, for the Lord, the fountain of joy and exultation, has dwelt in their midst]. St. Augustine sees that the praise here is not with the tongue only but with the whole life of man.

entries.section: 3. Jerusalem and the Incarnation:

paragraphs.text: And the joy does not stop at the man returning from captivity, but extends to his brethren whom he draws with him into the Kingdom of joy, for the prophet says: “And many nations shall be joined to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people: and I will dwell in the midst of thee” [11]. Here he speaks of the return of the Gentiles to the faith and their enjoying, together with their believing brethren of the Jews, God’s dwelling in the midst. And lest the Jews think that by this He has closed the door of faith in their face, He assured them: “And the LORD shall inherit Judah his portion in the holy land, and shall choose Jerusalem again.” If they become the new Judah by their being related to Him who came forth from the tribe of Judah, and if they become the new Jerusalem, they become the inheritance of the Lord and the place of His divine choice.

This work seems impossible in the eyes of all: how can the door be opened to all the nations, and they enjoy the dwelling of the Lord in their midst? Therefore He says: “Be silent, O all flesh, before the LORD: for he is raised up out of his holy habitation” [14]. Let every human tongue be silent in fear and trembling, for God, who has declared His care for all humanity through the generations, is working a wonder by opening the door of faith to the Gentiles, so that He appears as one who has awakened to raise humanity from its sleep!

entries.section: 1. Joshua and Satan:

paragraphs.text: “1 And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him. 2 And the LORD said unto Satan, ‘The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?’” [1-2].

What does this vision mean? The high priest was a symbol of the service of the temple, and by his captivity in Babylon the destruction of all the service of the temple appeared. But behind this lies a hidden enmity, not between Babylon and the high priest, but between the devil and God. Satan stood at the right hand of Joshua to resist him, but Joshua understands that the war is against God Himself, therefore he said: “The LORD rebuke thee.”

“The LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee”: not because of any merit on her part or any righteousness in her of herself, nor because she met the bitterness of captivity, but because God in His love chose her. As the Lord Christ assured His disciples: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you” (Jn 15:16). He is zealous over us because of His love for us, especially as He sees Satan as “a brand plucked out of the fire,” whose work is to cast himself into us to make of us a furnace that is never quenched.

Who is Joshua the son of Jehozadak the great priest? The Fathers see in Joshua a type of Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest and Bishop of our souls. For the word “Jesus” is shortened from Joshua, that is, “Jeho-salvation,” while “Jehozadak” means “God is righteousness.” Our Lord Jesus came to us as God our Savior and our righteousness; He came bearing our nature, so Satan did not perceive His true identity but doubted about Him, especially as He hungered and thirsted and suffered... So he stood at His right hand to resist Him, and the Lord overcame him and triumphed over him on our behalf.

The Lord Christ fought Satan, who is “a brand plucked out of the fire,” the destructive brand that men chose for themselves, which inflamed them with the fire of deadly passions. As St. Clement of Alexandria says: [Why do men flee to this deadly brand and die by it, when it is possible for them to live honored in God?!]. St. Didymus the Blind sees that Satan is a brand plucked out of the fire, which God could have left to burn without plucking it out, but He did not allow him to be punished with the full punishment for the present; rather He plucked him out to use him for His divine purposes, without Satan bearing fruit, like a branch struck by the fire to which life does not return. The Lord uses him as an instrument in which He is glorified by the victory of His children over him.

entries.section: 2. Joshua and the fair mitre:

paragraphs.text: 3 Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel. 4 And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment. 5 And I said, Let them set a fair mitre upon his head. So they set a fair mitre upon his head, and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD stood by.

We should not wonder that Joshua appeared clothed in filthy garments and standing before the angel to hear the command issued: Take away the filthy garments from him, for Joshua is a type of Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God, who bore our filthy garments so that by His Cross our sins might be taken away from us, that we might bear His righteousness and be crowned.
St. Jerome says: [The Lord bore these garments, and so He gave the enemy the opportunity to stand before Him to resist Him; since He put on our sins, in this he is His adversary].

St. Didymus the Blind says: [After they took away the filthy garments from him they put the fair mitre on his head and clothed him with garments. For the sake of the re-establishment of the city and the temple and their building, the chief of the captives who were set free puts on the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness, saying: “My soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isa 61:10). The filthy garments are cast off from him, since he must no longer grieve but rejoice and exult in the salvation of those who endured captivity. But who are those to whom the command was given to take off from him the garments of sorrow, which were described as filthy..? It may be said that they are the angels who surround those who fear God, protect them, and keep them from feeling the anxiety and sorrow which the trials of life bring].
It was said to Joshua: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment” [3-4].

How is it said to him: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee”? Our teacher Paul the Apostle says: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor 5:21); “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree: that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith” (Gal 3:13-14). It is as though He bore what was ours of sins so that by the Cross He might remove them and we might bear His righteousness.

As for the adorned garment that the Lord put on in place of the filthy garments, it signifies His Church adorned with manifold gifts, like the coat of many colors that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Each one of us represents a thread in this garment; if it is pulled out, the garment loses its beauty and its strength. This is the garment in which the Lord is transfigured and becomes radiant as the light (Mt 17:2). As St. Augustine says: [His garments are the Church, for if the one who wears them does not hold them, they fall; in this garment Paul was as a hem, since he said of himself: “For I am the least of the apostles” (1 Cor 15:9)... Therefore the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, when she touched the hem of the garment of the Lord Christ, was healed. So the Church that came from the Gentiles became whole through the teachings of Paul the Apostle].

St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the putting off of the filthy garments and the putting on of the adorned garment signifies putting off our old man and our enjoyment of the new man through the waters of Baptism, as he says: [By this we learn in a symbolic way that in the baptism of the Lord Christ we put off our sins like a poor and filthy garment and put on the holy garment of renewal, which is most fitting].
As for the fair mitre, it is the crown with which we are crowned in the holy Lord.

entries.section: 3. Joshua, the worker in the house of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 6 And the angel of the LORD protested unto Joshua, saying, 7 “Thus saith the LORD of hosts; If thou wilt walk in my ways, and if thou wilt keep my charge, then thou shalt also judge my house, and shalt also keep my courts, and I will give thee places to walk among these that stand by. 8 Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, thou, and thy fellows that sit before thee: for they are men wondered at: for, behold, I will bring forth my servant the BRANCH. 9 For behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes: behold, I will engrave the graving thereof, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day. 10 In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, shall ye call every man his neighbour under the vine and under the fig tree.”

entries.section: 3. Joshua, the worker in the house of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: The commandment presented to us has become directed to our Head and Great High Priest, Jesus Christ: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts; If thou wilt walk in my ways, and if thou wilt keep my charge, then thou shalt also judge my house, and shalt also keep my courts, and I will give thee places to walk among these that stand by” [7]. The secret of presenting the commandment to Him is that we cannot carry it out except through Him, and we cannot fulfil the charges of God without His work in us.

If the Church is the house of God, then our Lord Jesus is the One who judges the Church, upholding those who stand and raising the fallen; thus His children are “standing,” that is, risen in Him, and He finds for Himself a way to walk among them.

Finally He concludes this vision by revealing the person of this great priest: “For, behold, I will bring forth my servant the Branch, the East is his name: for behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes: behold, I will engrave the graving thereof, saith the LORD of hosts, shall ye call every man his neighbour under the vine and under the fig tree” [8-15].
We can summarize His discourse here about the person of our Lord Jesus Christ as follows:

First: He calls Him: My servant, the Branch, the East, the Stone; each title completes the rest of the titles. Through the Incarnation He became a servant, for He “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Phil 2:6-7). And by His descent from David the king He came forth as a branch, though He is the Creator of the vine (Isa 11:1-2); as for His being called the East, it is because He is the Sun of Righteousness who shines upon those sitting in darkness. And finally He was called the Stone, since the builders rejected Him and He became the chief cornerstone, joining Jews and Gentiles together in the heavenly spiritual building of which the Apostle said: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20).

Second: He says: “I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day,” which is the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ as the Sun that has risen upon us without setting, turning our night into a day without night; in Him our iniquities were taken away by the Cross.

Third: In that day, the day of the Cross, we were bound together: “shall ye call every man his neighbour under the fig tree,” that is, our being bound together in Him by love through His Church, the holy vine and the fruitful fig tree. In our study of the Book of Hosea we saw how the vine signifies the suffering Church that passes through the winepress with her Bridegroom, and the fig tree the unity of the Holy Spirit, who is indicated by the fig's husk which contains within it many seeds that have no value except through the unity of the Spirit.

entries.section: 1. Awakening the prophet:

paragraphs.text: “And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep.” [1].

Perhaps the sleep of Zechariah the prophet reveals the distress of soul of Zerubbabel, who found resistance from outside and inside, and since the prophet Zechariah could not support him, he slept. Perhaps by this he played the same role that the disciples played in the garden, who did not endure the events from merely hearing about them, so they slept, and the Lord came to rebuke them, addressing Peter the Apostle: “Couldest not thou watch one hour? Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation” (Mk 14:37-38).

entries.section: 2. The golden lampstand:

paragraphs.text: 2 And said unto me, What seest thou? And I said, I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof: 3 And two olive trees by it, one upon the right side of the bowl, and the other upon the left side thereof. 4 So I answered and spake to the angel that talked with me, saying, What are these, my lord? 5 Then the angel that talked with me answered and said unto me, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. 6 Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. 7 Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the corner stone amid those who cry, Honor, honor to him.

Since the house was being rebuilt by the hands of Zerubbabel, the thought of the prophet and of all the faithful in the service of the Lord soared, floating in the glory of this house and of what it contained of furnishings, especially the golden ones that the Lord commanded Moses to prepare, among them the golden lampstand with its seven lamps. In this vision God drew the heart of the prophet to see the return of the golden lampstand, which represents the illumination of the temple with the oil of divine grace and the work of the Holy Spirit. But this lampstand differed in some of its details from the traditional lampstand (Ex 37:17-24), and two olive trees surrounded it here, one on the right of the bowl of the lampstand and the other on its left.

entries.section: Note the following about this lampstand:

paragraphs.text: First: The lampstand is golden, that is, heavenly and spiritual, a symbol of the Church (Rev 1:20), and it bears the heavenly character, so it needs its heavenly Bridegroom Himself as its helper and keeper. As St. Didymus the Blind says: [When he says that the lampstand is all gold [2], it shows us that the lampstand that is wholly filled with light is a spiritual, not a material, lampstand. This golden lampstand represents the dwelling of God and His temple, as it is written in the Book of Revelation: “The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches” (Rev 1:20)].

Second: He says: “a bowl upon the top of it.” It is as though this lampstand represents the Church enlightened by the Holy Spirit, which the Lord Christ likens to five wise virgins who carried oil in their vessels and went out to meet the bridegroom (Mt 25). St. Augustine sees in this oil the love of God and of one's neighbor, which the Holy Spirit pours out abundantly in us. Whoever has the love of God in him carries the divine light and enjoys the Kingdom, while whoever loses love is in darkness and cannot behold God.
Third: “and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof” [2].

entries.section: Note the following about this lampstand:

paragraphs.text: St. Didymus the Blind says: [As the bowl is above the lampstand, so the seven lamps appear above it, so that the light is multiplied seven times, because just as perfect luminous knowledge has been likened to seven eyes [9], and just as the seven pillars bear the dwelling of wisdom: “Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars” (Prov 9:1), so the lampstand bears seven lamps. And the lampstand represents the Lord the Savior since it is all gold, because the Lord “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet 2:22), and there rests upon Him like seven lamps: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of divine counsel and might, of knowledge and godliness and the fear of the Lord (Isa 11:2)].

And the Church also, since she bears the characteristics of her Bridegroom and enjoys His righteousness, becomes a golden lampstand without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27), her light not from herself but the light of her Bridegroom the “Sun of Righteousness,” who shines without setting, He who sent to her His Holy Spirit to enlighten her in the midst of the world. As for the seven pipes, they are the means of salvation through which the Holy Spirit works in the Church, especially the seven Sacraments. This is the essence of the vision: the confirmation of the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church, as He says: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain” [6-7].

From the historical side, the resistance against Zerubbabel was like a great mountain that no human arm could move, until Zerubbabel doubted the completion of the work, but the Lord assured him that He Himself would complete the work [8]. God turned this great mountain before him into a plain. From the spiritual side, the disciples also needed the Holy Spirit so that the great mountain of preaching might become a plain, for the Lord said to them: “But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1:4-8).

If we may say that the preaching of the Crucified among the Jews was a stumblingblock and foolishness (1 Cor 1:23), as though it were a great mountain, then by the Holy Spirit this mountain became a plain before the Apostles and disciples. Therefore the Lord continues His speech: “and he shall bring forth the corner stone amid those who cry, Honor, honor to him” [7]. It is as though the work of the Holy Spirit in them is the witness to the Lord Christ, the cornerstone who bound Jews and Gentiles together in Himself, and all cry out, “Honor, honor to him.” As for the repetition of the word “honor,” it signifies the people who are of two origins, Jewish and Gentile, and it also signifies the nature of love that belongs to the new people, for St. Augustine sees that the number 2 signifies love, so no one can witness to the Crucified and glorify Him unless he bears in him this loving nature.

St. Didymus the Blind says: [Apart from the interpretation we presented, there is another view which says that the mountain symbolizes the Virgin Mary, and the stone coming out of it symbolizes Christ whom she bore without marriage, and the prophet Daniel teaches us these mysteries, saying: “Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces” (Dan 2:34). He says that the stone that smites the various kingdoms and the image that it formed was cut out of the mountain without the help of hands, done without the work of parents... and Christ alone is the One who was born of a virgin. Before Zerubbabel the stone was cut out of the mountain without the help of hands].

If this great mountain is the Lady the Virgin who bore the Lord Christ without the seed of man, a matter that seemed impossible yet was fulfilled, then it also signifies the soul that bears within it the Lord Christ spiritually, as St. Cyril the Great says: [Through the Spirit Christ is formed in us and stamps His features on us, and thus the beauty of His divinity becomes alive again in the nature of man].

Fourth: “And two olive trees by it, one upon the right side of the bowl, and the other upon the left side thereof” [3]. Perhaps these two olive trees signify Zerubbabel and Joshua, anointed to rebuild the temple, for they are the “sons of oil” [14]. One carries out the material role and the other the spiritual work, without duality, but each completes the other and supports him.

If the oil signifies the work of the Holy Spirit who enlightens the soul with true knowledge, then the olive tree on the right, in the view of St. Didymus, signifies the knowledge of divine things, while the second signifies the study of the world and its order and the arrangement of divine providence for it.

St. Didymus also sees that the two olive trees signify Moses and Elijah, who appeared on the right and on the left of the Lord at the moments of the Transfiguration (Lk 9:30), since the Law is spiritual, a son of anointing, and the word of prophecy is also spiritual; and the two witness to the glory of the Lord and His divinity.
Perhaps the two olive trees signify the Holy Bible with its two Testaments, for the Holy Spirit uses it to enlighten our heart with the light of knowledge and the manifestation of the Lord within us.

entries.section: 3. The completion of the work:

paragraphs.text: 8 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 9 The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you. 10 For who hath despised the day of small things? Those seven shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth. 11 Then answered I, and said unto him, What are these two olive trees upon the right side of the candlestick and upon the left side thereof? 12 And I answered again, and said unto him, What be these two olive branches which through the two golden pipes empty the golden oil out of themselves? 13 And he answered me and said, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. 14 Then said he, These are the two sons of oil, that stand by the LORD of the whole earth.
This vision came to give Zerubbabel assurance regarding the following:
First: The work is not accomplished by a human arm but by the Spirit of God [6-7].

entries.section: 3. The completion of the work:

paragraphs.text: Second: God confirms the completion of the work by the hand of Zerubbabel, even if it remained suspended for years because of the resistance [9].

entries.section: 3. The completion of the work:

paragraphs.text: Third: God rejoices in the work that many despised when they compared it with the first temple, counting it [small things] [10]... In their eyes it is a small work, indeed as nothing (Hag 2:3), but God rejoices in it as His seven eyes, roving through the whole earth, look upon it, not to criticize and condemn but to rejoice in the work of the children of God and strengthen their hands (2 Chr 16:9). The eyes of the Lord see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel [10], that is, they see him holding the instrument that measures the straightness of the building (which was usually of lead in the form of a weight tied to a string).

entries.section: 1. The flying scroll:

paragraphs.text: 1 Then I turned, and lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a flying roll. 2 And he said unto me, What seest thou? And I answered, I see a flying roll; the length thereof is twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof ten cubits. 3 Then said he unto me, This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the whole earth: for every one that stealeth shall be cut off as on this side according to it; and every one that sweareth shall be cut off as on that side according to it. 4 I will bring it forth, saith the LORD of hosts, and it shall enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him that sweareth falsely by my name: and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof.
The prophet lifted up his eyes and saw a flying scroll (a sheet), and as it came in the Septuagint, “a flying sickle.”

entries.section: 1. The flying scroll:

paragraphs.text: The scroll often signifies the proclamation of judgment (Ezek 2:9-10; Rev 5:1; 10:2). Though the people of God appeared in the previous vision as a lampstand all of gold, bearing the light of Christ with the oil of the Holy Spirit, its joy in this divine work is accompanied by caution against every sin or carelessness. As for its flying, it is because the evil we commit here ascends before God as a corrupt odor, so it pours out a curse “over the face of the whole earth” [3]. Here God declares the responsibility of the believer as a member of the whole human community, interacting either for blessing or for curse. What he does has an effect on the life of all; for because of Joseph the house of Potiphar was blessed and the storehouses of Egypt were blessed, and because of the flight of Jonah the sea was stirred up and many lost their goods.

And the wonder is that the prophet sees evil as a sheet flying open, its length twenty cubits and its breadth ten cubits. On the earth it was folded and no one knew its hidden things, but it will not remain so; rather it will be exposed, and all will be able to read it. As for its dimensions, they are proportionate to the dimensions of the tabernacle or the Holy Place, as though what man commits corrupts the holy things of God in him.

But in the Septuagint the prophet sees a flying sickle, and as St. Didymus the Blind says: [Since the Judge separates the righteous from the wicked and repays each one according to his deeds, therefore Holy Scripture calls the retributions under which the unjust and the wicked fall sometimes a sword and an arrow (Deut 32:42; 22:23; Isa 34:5; Amos 9:10; Ps 7:12-13; Jer 47:5-6) and sometimes an axe and a sickle... For the trees that bear no good fruit become the object of wrath and punishment (they are struck with the axe and the sickle)... So it is said: “And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire” (Mt 3:10). Thus the curse comes upon plants of this kind. And thus the sickle is also used to cut down those who bear corrupt fruits, of whom it was said: “For their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves being judges. For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps” (Deut 32:31-33). Thus the evil will is likened to the corrupt vine that bears bad fruit and must be cut with a sharp sickle and its grapes and clusters removed... The prophet sees it as a flying sickle, not an ordinary sickle but, without doubt, a spiritual one... It cuts down “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted” (Mt 15:13), that is, “it cuts down everything unclean.”

St. John Chrysostom comments on this sharp sickle, saying: [Perhaps a man might escape a flying sword, but from a sickle that comes down upon his neck and winds around it like a rope binding it, he cannot escape. And if wings are added to the sickle, what hope of rescue can be found?!]. He also says: [It is flying, indicating the swiftness of the coming of vengeance... As for its length and breadth being many cubits, it means the severity and enormity of the woes. It flies from heaven, meaning the coming of vengeance from the judgment seat on high, and in the form of a sickle for the inevitability of judgment. For just as the sickle that comes upon the neck and takes hold of it does not return empty but cuts off the head, so vengeance will be severe and sure].

The prophet continues his speech: “Then said he unto me, This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the whole earth: for every one that stealeth shall be cut off as on this side according to it; and every one that sweareth shall be cut off as on that side according to it. I will bring it forth, saith the LORD of hosts, and it shall enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him that sweareth falsely by my name: and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof” [3-4].

The Mosaic covenant carried with it a curse that comes upon the disobedient (Deut 27:15-26; 28:15-68); this curse hovers in the air and threatens the inhabitants of the earth who took the covenant and did not keep it but betrayed it. Here two sins are emphasized: theft and false swearing. By the first a man robs his brother and by the second he despises God, as though the two sins include the breaking of the whole Law: the violation of the right of the brethren and of God. Perhaps the commandment concerning not stealing was in the middle of the second tablet, and that concerning not swearing falsely in the middle of the first, meaning that man breaks the two tablets in their depths.

Though the curse touches the whole face of the earth, yet as it flies it strikes its arrow at the house of the wrongdoer himself, to lodge there and destroy it, with its timber and its stones; he receives the natural fruit of his work. St. Didymus the Blind says: [This sickle flies and traverses the whole earth swiftly, striking not only the sinners who are on the earth but also those in the air (the demons) and the wicked wherever they are found. It destroys what is in the midst of the house, that is, the heart and the mind, and it shatters what is within man like the sword that cut in two from the middle the judge of Israel who was burning with the passion of adultery with Susanna: “For, behold, the angel of God hath received sentence of God to cut thee in two” (Additions to Dan 13:55), so cutting the adulterer from the middle means the division of his mind.
