Among the words of St. John Chrysostom: [He who governs others must be more radiant than any shining star; his life must be without blemish; all look to him and see in his life a model for themselves].

Third: He continues His speech, saying: "execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates"... If "truth" is the foundation on which the new city is built, then it is fitting that truth be mixed with peace. Heavenly truth opens the heart with love so that it is wide enough to bear with others, being at peace, if possible, with all men.

St. Didymus the Blind comments on His saying "in your gates," saying that the courts of justice founded on truth mixed with peace are at the gates, to sort those entering the city from those who are barred from it. It is as though peace does not mean flattery at the expense of truth or leniency toward evil, but while the heart is widened with love, nothing defiled or abominable must enter the holy city!
Let us love all and open our hearts to peace with all, but let us not open our inner gates to evil and sin out of courtesy to others!

Fourth: "let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour," meaning the inner forgetting of every wrong a neighbor has done to us, or not thinking ill of his actions. Joseph the Righteous presents to us a living example of this virtue; in his composure he realizes what his brothers did to him, but his heart sees beyond his brothers' actions: the hand of God working for his salvation and theirs; therefore with a wide heart he said to them: "God did send me before you to preserve life" (Gen 45:5) "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive" (Gen 50:20).

When a man realizes the divine purposes his soul rests greatly in everything, and his heart is widened with peace for everyone, even for his opponents, so he does not resist evil with evil but with good and with love.
Fifth: Finally He asks them not to love a false oath, which the Lord hates, since He commanded us: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain" (Ex 20:7).

entries.section: 4. The fasts turn into feasts:

paragraphs.text: 18 And the word of the LORD of hosts came unto me, saying, 19 "Thus saith the LORD of hosts; The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness, and cheerful feasts; therefore love the truth and peace.

"The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness, and cheerful feasts; therefore love the truth and peace" [18-19].

Their past life had been marked by fasting with mourning because of the chastenings that came upon them for their sins; and now that the Lord dwells in their midst and declares His dwelling in them, He turns their hearts to joy and their life to an unceasing feast. So also the true Christian in the midst of his fasts and sufferings, as he realizes the indwelling of God in him, inner joy does not cease from him and the feast does not stop in his life.

In the previous chapter we spoke about fasting as not merely abstaining from food but stopping from evil together with enjoying the Lord Christ, the bread of life. This concerns spiritual fasting; as for the feast, St. Athanasius the Apostolic says: [Jesus Christ, who is the way and the door and everything for us, is also "our feast," as the blessed Paul says: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7)]. And as fasting is not merely abstaining from foods, so the feast is not eating and drinking but a joyful life in the Lord. Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says: [Let us not keep the feast in an earthly manner but as those who keep a feast in heaven with the angels... Let us rejoice not in ourselves but in the Lord, so that we may be with the saints]. [Let us not stop at merely performing the rites of the feast but prepare to draw near to the divine Lamb and touch the heavenly food].

entries.section: 5. Their dwelling a blessing for the nations:

paragraphs.text: 20 Thus saith the LORD of hosts; It shall yet come to pass, that there shall come people, and the inhabitants of many cities: 21 And the inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, Let us go speedily to pray before the LORD, and to seek the LORD of hosts: I will go also. 22 Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem, and to pray before the LORD. 23 "Thus saith the LORD of hosts; In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you."

God does not accept half measures: either one is a curse to himself as to others, or a blessing to himself as to his brethren, for He says: "And it shall come to pass, that as ye were a curse among the heathen, O house of Judah, and house of Israel; so will I save you, and ye shall be a blessing" [13]. And here He explains to them how they will be a blessing, saying: "Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem, and to pray before the LORD... In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you" [22-23].

First: When God's wrath came upon them and the captivity took place, they became a curse among the nations; and the sign of this curse is the ruin of Jerusalem even in the days of the feast, as Jeremiah says lamenting Zion: "The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh" (Lam 1:4). And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [How should the ways of Zion not mourn, when no one comes to her and there is none to hasten in going up to Jerusalem to celebrate the feast and to assemble there...?!]. But now that she has turned from curse to blessing she has drawn many peoples to her so that they may enjoy the feast and rejoice in the Lord. Zechariah the prophet says: "Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem." And since Jerusalem means "vision of peace," the sign of blessing is the drawing of many to enjoy this spiritual vision of reconciliation on the Cross and obtaining peace with God.

Second: St. Didymus the Blind comments on the saying: "I will go also." He says that the prophet, seeing crowds of peoples and nations coming from Jerusalem, had his heart set aflame with longing, and desired to be among those coming, declaring it by his saying: "I will go also." He also sees that the speaker here is the Savior, who declares His entrance into Jerusalem, leading these peoples in the spirit of victory, saying: "I have raised him up with victory, and I will make all his ways smooth; he shall build my city, and shall release my captives, not for price nor for reward, saith the LORD of hosts" (Isa 45:13). As He opens the door, the door of victory and triumph, and builds the inner holy city, and frees the soul from its captivity not by a material price or an earthly reward but by His precious blood, the peoples and nations seek the Lord and enter the new Jerusalem to entreat the Lord's favor, those of whom the Apostle said: "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven" (Heb 12:22-23).

Third: The Lord does not say that He blesses them but what is greater: "ye shall be a blessing"; through them the nations are blessed, and in Zephaniah He says that they become "a praise among all the peoples of the earth" (Zeph 3:20), and in Micah they become "as a dew from the LORD" (Mic 5:7). So he who carries the Lord in his heart carries a blessing for others, and is a song of joy by which their hearts rejoice in the Lord; they become like the heavenly dew that quenches the flame of the world's destructive fire!

Fourth: He concludes His speech about the blessing with the fact that ten men from all languages of the nations take hold of the skirt of a Jewish man, saying, We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you. This is a picture of the bride who says in the Song: "Draw me, we will run after thee" (Song 1:4), for as she sets out toward her Bridegroom she carries with her ten persons whom she gains for the Lord by her holy life and her witness for the Lord. This from one side, and from another side we who were formerly of the Gentiles do not deny that we have received from them the Old Testament with what it contains of the Law and the prophecies as a way to the knowledge of salvation in Christ Jesus. We are indebted to them for receiving the faith in the Messiah the Savior.

St. Didymus the Blind sees that this Jew by whose skirt ten men from all the nations take hold is none other than the Lord Christ, who came forth from the tribe of Judah (Heb 7:14), as was said by Isaiah the prophet: "And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious" (Isa 11:10). He is the object of expectation not of one nation but of all the nations.

As for the number ten, it signifies, in the opinion of St. Didymus the Blind, the believers who have become ten virgins (Mt 25:1), having five holy senses of the body and five holy inner senses. As for these, since the believers bear the name "Jesus Christ," the beginning of His name is the letter "Iota," which is equivalent to the number 10 in the Greek language.

entries.section: 1. The victories of Alexander the Great:

paragraphs.text: 1 The burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof. For the LORD has the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel. 2 And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise. 3 And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets. 4 Behold, the Lord will possess her, and smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire. 5 Ashkelon shall see it, and fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed; and the king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. 6 And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines. 7 And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, shall be for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite. 8 And I will encamp about mine house because of the army that goeth and returneth, so that no collector of tribute shall pass over them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes.
He presents an oracle, a prophecy that carries a threat against the resisting nations and reassurance for those who rely on God.

First: Alexander the Great's attitude toward the cities of Syria and Phoenicia: "The burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof. For the LORD has the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel. And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise. And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets. Behold, the Lord will possess her, and smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire" [1-4].

Alexander the Great defeated a number of the cities of Syria, among them Hadrach, which is on the river Orontes not far from Hamath, but his eyes were on Damascus, the capital. The terror and amazement caused by his victories had drawn the eyes of the children of Israel to God, asking divine help from Him. As for Hamath, which is next to Damascus, it fell before him.

After Syria, Alexander entered Phoenicia and subdued Tyre, which was very rich through its trade, so that silver was to it like dust and gold like worthless mire; its inhabitants were compelled to fortify themselves on an island opposite Tyre, but Alexander burned the ancient city with fire and cast its stones into the sea to build a causeway by which he crossed to the island and besieged its fortresses, and they collapsed before him.

St. Didymus the Blind sees in Damascus and the other lands of Syria a symbolic picture of the nations that resisted the truth and then returned and accepted it, since it is said here: "Behold, the Lord will possess her"... He restores her from her former savagery to gentleness. As for Tyre, with its massive wall in which she fortified herself, it signifies the heretics who fortify themselves with sophistical arguments as their strongholds, but God also works to subject them to the true faith.

Tyre in truth represents the man who has become rich (Rev 3:17) and thought that he is able by himself to fortify himself and by his wealth to be satisfied; but as he gathers silver it becomes to him dust, and as he stores gold it becomes to him mire. The word of God, which is silver in itself, is turned to dust for him because of his earthly mind, and the spiritual life, which is heaven in itself, is turned to mire because of his descent to material things. He falls into the sea, which symbolizes the whirlpools of the world and the storms of anxiety and grief, and is devoured by the destroying fire, as sin crushes him and scatters his life and possessions! Wretched is this man who thinks himself very wise, as Tyre thought, and so ruined her silver and gold and cast herself into the sea of the love of the world and the destroying furnace of sin!

entries.section: 1. The victories of Alexander the Great:

paragraphs.text: Second: Alexander's attitude toward the cities of Philistia: "Ashkelon shall see it, and fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed..." [5]. In this passage and what follows it four Philistine cities are mentioned (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod), and the fifth of the principal cities, "Gath," is not mentioned, perhaps because it had not been rebuilt after it fell at the hand of Uzziah (2 Chr 26:6). Ashkelon feared and Gaza was very sorrowful, and Ekron also, when they saw what had befallen Tyre, the great fortified city, and realized the danger that was coming upon them.

These four cities, "Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod," signify the world with its four directions, which was filled with the pagan world, haughty, yet it comes back and returns to the Lord the Savior and enjoys salvation. These cities also signify earthly man, bound to the earth (the four quarters of the world), who has returned to his Savior bearing the spiritual mark.
"Ashkelon" is a Hebrew word derived from "shekel," that is, weight; "Gaza" means "might" or "strength"; "Ekron" means "barrenness"; "Ashdod" means "stiff, or ravager."

So Ashkelon signifies the soul that prides itself on its weight and measure; when the fear of the Lord comes upon it, it realizes itself and returns to the Lord that He may be everything to it, as the Psalmist says that those who fear the Lord "shall not want any good thing" (Ps 34:10).
And Gaza is very sorrowful [5]; what she counted might and strength she sees as nothing, so she receives the Lord Himself as her might and strength and inner glory.

And Ekron, as she realizes her barrenness, returns in contrition to the Lord her Savior, and He grants her blessed children (spiritual fruits), as the Psalmist says: "He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children" (Ps 113:9), and as it was said: "so that the barren hath born seven; and she that hath many children is waxed feeble" (1 Sam 2:5). This is the Church of the Gentiles, which was barren and bore many, while the company of the Jews, the possessors of the promises and covenants, among whom were the Fathers and prophets, withered because of its rejection of the Savior. Isaiah the prophet says: "Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife" (Isa 54:1). And as St. Didymus the Blind says: ["The married wife" (Baal) here is the Law; so the Gentiles, who were without the Law of Moses, were filled with joy at salvation, and the Jews, who had the Law, fell into the spiritual depth.

As for "Ashdod," when she realizes her corrupting stiffness and its destructive work she returns to the Lord and becomes subject to Him. Her god Dagon falls before the ark of the covenant (1 Sam 5) and her resistance to the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem ends (Neh 4:7), so that she receives the preaching of the Gospel by Philip (Acts 8:40) and becomes an episcopal see carrying out the preaching of salvation.

entries.section: 1. The victories of Alexander the Great:

paragraphs.text: The prophet speaks of what happens in Ashdod, saying: "And a bastard (illegitimate sons) shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines. And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, shall be for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite" [6-7]. This was fulfilled literally, for Ashdod almost lost its native inhabitants, since it was the policy of Alexander the Great to mix the conquered peoples together so as to deprive them of their national feeling. As for taking away the blood from the mouth, it signifies their abandoning idolatry, in which they ate the sacrifices with their blood (Ezek 33:25). The Law prohibited that (Lev 17:10-11; Acts 9:4). Ashdod returned to the Lord by accepting the Christian faith and her original dignity was restored to her, so she became as a governor in Judah, as Ekron, that is, the barren, became as a Jebusite in that she treads the love of the world under her feet.

entries.section: 1. The victories of Alexander the Great:

paragraphs.text: Third: Alexander's attitude toward the Jews: "And I will encamp about mine house because of the army that goeth and returneth, so that no collector of tribute shall pass over them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes" [8]. The Lord encamped about His house so that the army of Alexander the Great would not touch it in its repeated passing through Jerusalem, for he did not harm the Jews although he humbled the Samaritans. Josephus the Jewish historian mentions that Jaddua the high priest met Alexander with all the priests wearing the holy garments, the high priest wearing the turban on his head and the golden plate on which was written "Holiness to the LORD"; when Alexander saw him he bowed down to him and told him that he had seen in a dream the God whose name was written on the plate, then he entered Jerusalem and offered sacrifices and gave the Jews special privileges.

The Lord ends His speech here by saying: "for now have I seen with mine eyes." And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [This clear vision is the power of insight of which the Apostle writes: "all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13)]... as if what the Lord declares through the prophet is uncovered to the Lord, the Planner of our salvation!

entries.section: 2. The Messiah, the spiritual King:

paragraphs.text: 9 Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and victorious, and lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. 10 And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth. 11 As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water. 12 Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare that I will render double unto thee.

Lest some think that Zechariah aims at the salvation of the Macedonian age and the Lord's giving grace to the Jews in the eyes of Alexander, he moves on to the true salvation through the meek King, the Savior, the giver of peace to the world. God's open eyes behold His work of salvation as a present work by which humanity is saved; therefore He says: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and victorious, and lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth" [9-10].

A people deprived of its land for a long time and subjected under foreign kings in captivity: behold, its King comes to it, who makes the daughter of Zion rejoice greatly and gladdens the heart of the daughter of Jerusalem. He is a wonderful King, as St. John Chrysostom says: [He does not lead chariots like the rest of kings, nor demand tribute, nor drive people away, nor ask for guards, but walks in His great meekness].

We presented previously, in the commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew, the thought of the Fathers of the Church in interpreting this text and the symbols that the colt and the ass carried when the Lord rode them at His entry into Jerusalem, and the symbols that Jerusalem carried in receiving the Lord with rejoicing. And here we notice:

First: St. Didymus the Blind sees that the word "Zion" means "observer of the commandments or one who carries them out," while Jerusalem means "vision of peace," as if those who enjoy gladness and exultation at the Lord's entry into their lives are the doers of the commandments and those who enjoy the vision of peace (through the Cross). The Psalmist says: "The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes" (Ps 119:8). "By the first (carrying out the commandment) the soul rejoices greatly at the coming of the true King, and by the second (the vision of peace) she shouts because she is in a very elevated position announcing the coming of the King of kings... The first received a command to rejoice and the second received a command to proclaim it!

May we truly be the daughter of Zion and so rejoice greatly through our keeping of the divine commandment, and let us be the daughter of Jerusalem and shout, declaring witness to Him through our vision of the true peace that surpasses all in the crucified Lord!

Second: As the meek Lord the Savior enters the heart, He cuts off the war chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem and removes the battle bow, so that peace comes within, and Ephraim becomes fruitful and Jerusalem enjoys true peace, singing: "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God. They are brought down and fallen: but we are risen, and stand upright" (Ps 20:7-8).

Third: The dominion of the Lord the King extends over the nations, from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Perhaps by the seas He means those who used to drink salt water through pagan teachings, while by the river He means the holy Law of Moses, so He brings the Gentiles together with the Jews under His dominion.

entries.section: 2. The Messiah, the spiritual King:

paragraphs.text: Fourth: He says: "As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water. Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I cry that I will render double unto thee" [11-12]. It seems that Israel, as a company of farmers, each group of them had hewn a pit for themselves among the rocks so that when the time of rain came it would fill with water; so when the time of captivity came and they entered into a state of terror they fled from the enemies to the pit in which there was no water and became prisoners there. Perhaps this pit signifies the human self which man establishes by himself to confine himself in it by himself, but God releases him by the covenant of the holy blood, releases him from his selfishness and his self that he may live in the fullness of the freedom of the Cross. And St. Didymus the Blind sees in this pit without water, into which Joseph and Jeremiah and Daniel, etc., were cast, a sign of Hades, which has no water of eternal life, from which the Lord has released us not through the blood of bulls and goats but through the blood of the New Covenant. He calls us to come out of the pit to go forth to the stronghold, which is the glorious Church without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27). "There the captives drawn out of the pit without water find rest." For in the Church the Lord's prisoners find "a stronghold for uprightness is the way of the LORD" (Prov 10:29), and the Lord Himself is a stronghold: "Be thou to me a rock of refuge, whereunto I may continually resort" (Ps 71:3), "Be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me. For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name's sake lead me, and guide me" (Ps 31:2-3).

Sixth: God restores to the soul a double reward in place of the days of its toil, and as St. Didymus the Blind says: [He who is a prisoner of Christ settles in this city and sits in the glorious strongholds within it, and lives without fear as he awaits double consolations and encouragement in place of sorrow... The reward will be double for the former afflictions, and the clear example of that is the story of Job, who had a strong soul and so received a double reward (Job 42:11)]. He receives a double reward, as he enjoys a hundredfold in this world and eternal life in the world to come; it is also double since he receives the salvation of the soul together with the body. And the secret of its doubling, as St. Didymus the Blind says: [He who is in captivity, when he returns from his captivity, is not only saved but becomes a teacher of his oppressors, so his glory is doubled glory!]

entries.section: 3. The victories of the Maccabees:

paragraphs.text: 13 For I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Javan, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man. 14 And the LORD shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord GOD shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south. 15 The LORD of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and tread upon sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar. 16 And the LORD their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land. 17 For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! corn shall make the young men grow, and new wine the maids.

After speaking of the victories of Alexander the Great and how God gave favor to the Jews in his eyes, and then returning to tell us of the Messiah King, he speaks here of "Javan," that is, the Greeks, since the Maccabees defeated them in the second century before the Nativity (Dan 11:32; 8:9-14), and the prophecy came to affirm one thing: that God is the secret of their victory.

He says "I have bent Judah for me" [13]; what is this arrow that goes forth from Judah to raise up the sons of Zion against the sons of Javan but the Lord Christ Himself, the divine arrow going forth from the tribe of Judah on behalf of the sons of faith against the devil and his evil works?! He is the word of the living and effective God, sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb 4:12), who says: "he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword" (Isa 49:2).

entries.section: 3. The victories of the Maccabees:

paragraphs.text: As the arrow was launched on behalf of the salvation of humanity against the devil, the Lord was manifested in His kingdom, and as the prophet says: "And the LORD shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord GOD shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south. The LORD of hosts shall defend them" [14-15]. The Lord Christ, the true arrow, has gone forth like lightning; He enters the heart and wounds it with the wounds of love, so that the soul says: "I am sick of love" (Song 5:8); He destroys in it the works of the devil and flashes in it with the splendor of His glory. And as it is written in Habakkuk: "At the light of thine arrows that fly, at the shining of the lightning of thy glory" (Hab 3:11). And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [Jerusalem is Judah... as the divine arrow goes forth from it like lightning, the inner man is enlightened and the eyes of the heart are enlightened]. And as the Lord gives enlightenment to the eyes of the soul by the lightning, so the blowing of the trumpet gives an inner ear to hear His voice that resounds to warn us of the enemy the devil and to join us to the celebration of His joyful coming, since trumpets were sounded at war as at feasts.

entries.section: 3. The victories of the Maccabees:

paragraphs.text: Thus he prophesies about the victory over the Greeks by the Maccabees, and declares our eternal victory over the devil in Christ Jesus, the true divine arrow. He has depicted this victory for us by saying: "The LORD of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and tread upon sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar. And the LORD their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land. For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! corn shall make the young men grow, and new wine the maids" [15-16].

If God used the pagans as sling stones that He aimed at His people to chasten them, then when He returns to them with His mercy He makes these stones beneath them, which they tread with their feet; so in the same thought, if God allows us various trials or afflictions, He uses them for our discipline or our approval, and in His love does not make us fall under the trial, but the trial falls beneath us and has no authority over us to deprive us of our inner peace and our joy in the Lord.
And just as at the captivity the people drank the cup of God's wrath with sorrow and pain, so when God has compassion on them they drink the cup of gladness and joy!

He gives victory to His people as His rational flock, and sets them up as the stones of a crown lifted up upon His land, and according to the Septuagint He sets them up as holy stones rolling upon the earth. St. Jerome comments on this, saying: [Note His saying: "holy stones rolling upon the earth"; they are wheels that run upon the earth, hastening toward the high places]. He also says: ["A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together" (Eccl 3:5). Now God has raised up from the hard stones of the Gentiles children to Abraham (Mt 3:9), and they have become holy stones rolling upon the earth (Zech 9:16), which have passed through the winnowing fan of the air of the world and rolled in the chariot of God on swift wheels]. And when he spoke of Paula, who spent her money not on stone buildings but on the poor, he said: [She wished to spend her money not on the stones that pass away with the passing of the world but on the living stones that roll upon the earth, and by which the city of the great King is built, as it is said in the Book of Revelation (Rev 21:14)].

Through this surpassing victory that lifts the soul to heaven as living stones rolling upward to the Jerusalem above, the soul feels a spiritual satisfaction, for it is said "corn shall make the young men grow, and new wine the maids"... God offers Himself as wheat and new wine to satisfy our young men and young women, that is, to make the fruits of the Spirit grow in us through the sanctification of the soul with all its faculties (the young men) and the body with all its senses and emotions (the maids).

entries.section: 1. Enjoying the latter rain:

paragraphs.text: "Ask ye of the LORD rain in the time of the latter rain; so the LORD shall make lightnings, and give them showers of rain, to every one grass in the field" [1].

In ancient times, because of evil, Elijah stopped the rain for three years and six months so that all might be disciplined and the rain come down, and so our sins hold back the overflow of God's abundant graces upon us and deprive us of His rain that turns the barren wilderness into a garden that gladdens His heart (Song 5:1).

In our study of the Book of Hosea (6:3) we noticed that in Palestine an early rain falls where the seed is sown, and a latter rain by which the crop is ripened; the first rain signifies the work of the Holy Spirit through the Law and the prophecies, etc., before the coming of the Lord, while the latter signifies the abundance of the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Church of the New Covenant, which Joel the prophet announced: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh" (Joel 2:28).

We can say that the early rain is the Law and the prophecies that the Lord gave to the men of the Old Testament, while the latter rain is the preaching of the Gospel, which uncovers the mysteries of God and gives us deep knowledge and a vision of the divine life.
St. Didymus the Blind sees that the early rain also means the teachings concerning the Incarnation of the Savior, while the latter rain is the enjoyment of the mysteries of His divinity.

In any case, let us not cease to ask God without interruption that He may flash in our hearts with the splendor of His glory, giving us His latter rain to water our land with His divine love and give it multiplied fruit.

entries.section: 2. Enjoying God's personal care:

paragraphs.text: 2 For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie, and have told false dreams; they comfort in vain: therefore they went their way as a flock, they were humbled, because there was no shepherd. 3 "Mine anger was kindled against the shepherds, and I punished the he-goats: for the LORD of hosts hath visited his flock the house of Judah, and hath made them as his goodly horse in the battle.

Though God sends rain on the righteous and the wicked, He does not give the spiritual rain except to those who ask for it; and now, for Him to take care of His flock spiritually, this flock must abandon the deceptions of divination and sorcery and the dreams of the false prophets so that He Himself may shepherd His people.

"For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie, and have told false dreams; they deceive with vanity, therefore they went their way as a flock. They were humbled because there is no shepherd. Mine anger was kindled against the shepherds, and I punished the he-goats: for the LORD of hosts hath visited his flock the house of Judah, and hath made them as his goodly horse in the battle" [2-3].

The teraphim are statues of gods that they set up inside the houses as guardians for them and to consult before every action. God cannot take over the care of His people as long as they rely on the teraphim and ask divination and resort to the dreams of the false prophets, for all these may placate a man and deceive him with soft, deceptive words, but those who rely on them do not fall into humiliation, since they are without care. And now, as the people leave these vain deceptions, the Lord does two works: He declares His wrath against the corrupt shepherds and takes over the shepherding Himself, as He affirmed in the Book of Ezekiel: "Behold, I will inquire after my sheep and visit them... I will feed my flock, and I will cause them to lie down, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 34:11, 15). He punishes the evil he-goats (the rams) and takes care of His flock, giving His life as a ransom for it (Jn 10:11). He gives them His life that is able to set them up as a horse in the procession of salvation, able to fight against the devil and his works. And as it was said: "Was the LORD displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?" (Hab 3:8).

entries.section: 3. Enjoying victory and the restoration of the kingdom:

paragraphs.text: 4 Out of him is the corner, out of him the nail, out of him the battle bow, out of him shall come forth every oppressor together. 5 And they shall be as mighty men, treading the mire of the streets in the battle: and they shall fight, because the LORD is with them, and the riders on horses shall be confounded. 6 And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them again; for I have mercy upon them: and they shall be as though I had not cast them off: for I am the LORD their God, and will hear them. 7 And they of Ephraim shall be like a mighty man, and their heart shall rejoice as through wine: yea, their children shall see it, and be glad; their heart shall rejoice in the LORD. 8 I will whistle for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them: and they shall increase as they have increased. 9 And I will sow them among the people: and they shall remember me in far countries; and they shall live with their children, and turn again. 10 I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Assyria; and I will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon; and place shall not be found for them. 11 And he shall pass through the sea of affliction, and shall smite the depths in the sea, and all the deeps of the river shall dry up: and the pride of Assyria shall be brought down, and the sceptre of Egypt shall depart away. 12 And I will strengthen them in the LORD; and they shall walk in his name, saith the LORD.
The fruit of God's personal care is their enjoyment of victory and security and joy and the restoration of God's kingdom among them.

First: "Out of him is the corner, out of him the nail, out of him the battle bow, out of him shall come forth every oppressor speedily" [4]. True divine care appears in the manifestation of the Lord Christ among His people as a cornerstone that binds all together in Him and supports all with one spirit. He also appears among them as a nail (peg) that supports their temporal tent, that is, their temporary life, so that the winds of strange teachings do not move it nor the storms of the love of the world and the lusts of the flesh. This is the divine peg that supports the body (the tent) by its sanctification for the sake of the Kingdom of God. And the Lord is also among them a battle bow that the believer aims, fighting evil and sin, so that it is said of them: "One of you shall chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight" (Deut 32:30), and they, as soldiers of the Lord carrying the Lord Christ as their true arrow, say: "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places" (Eph 6:13).

As for His saying: "out of him shall come forth every oppressor speedily," it refers to His work in His Church, which receives Him as cornerstone and nail and spiritual bow, as He removes from it the oppressor and the corrupter so that all in it may be sanctified by Him.

entries.section: 3. Enjoying victory and the restoration of the kingdom:

paragraphs.text: Second: "And they shall be as mighty men, treading the mire of the streets in the battle: and they shall fight, because the LORD is with them, and the riders on horses shall be confounded" [5]. This is their might and this is their victory, that they tread the mire of the streets; so he is not like him who had the talent and buried it in the earth (Mt 25:18), but by the heavenly Lord they rise above every material thought, soaring in the heavenly places, however violent this thought may seem, like riders of horses.

St. Didymus the Blind distinguishes between riders of horses and horsemen; the riders of horses are those who mount them without controlling them with a bridle, for if horses signify the body, the soul mounts the body and leaves it in its unruliness and stubbornness, so this soul is put to shame because of the lusts of the body. The horses also signify arrogant sophistical thoughts which the soul mounts and so falls into pride and is deprived of salvation. Of the riders of horses it was said: "the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea" (Ex 15:1), "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God" (Ps 20:7), "An horse is a vain thing for safety" (Ps 33:7). This is concerning the riders of horses, while the horsemen signify him who mounts the horse or steed controlling it with a bridle, for it was said to Elijah the prophet: "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof" (2 Kgs 2:12).

entries.section: 3. Enjoying victory and the restoration of the kingdom:

paragraphs.text: Third: He compensates them for the years that the locust has eaten, so in place of the losses that befell them on the day the Lord rejected them they receive great blessings that cover the former losses, for He says: "And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them again; for I have mercy upon them: and they shall be as though I had not cast them off: for I am the LORD their God, and will hear them" [6]. Why does He speak of the house of Judah and the house of Joseph? Because from the first house came forth Jesus, the giver of salvation, and from the second house appeared Joseph, a type of Christ, who provided wheat after hunger and famine had crushed them (Gen 41:56). If Israel passed through years of famine, the true Joseph satisfies them, as St. Mary says: "He hath filled the hungry with good things" (Lk 1:53). He is the Lord their God who answers their request and satisfies their needs, so they no longer remember the past with its harsh spiritual famine, for the joys of the present cover all the sorrows of the past. Therefore He says: "And they of Ephraim shall be like a mighty man, and their heart shall rejoice as through wine" [7]. This is the mark of the messianic age: the joy of the Holy Spirit, which the world cannot take away from the heart!

Here he mentions Ephraim as a mighty man filled with joy, perhaps an allusion to the northern kingdom, which lived in captivity for a longer time than Judah, so He affirmed His support for it. Perhaps he meant the tribe of Ephraim in particular, because it was the violent one that was the first instigator of the corruption of the northern kingdom, especially as Jeroboam, who incited the ten tribes to rebel against Judah, was an Ephraimite (1 Kgs 11:26; 12:2), and it was he who established idol worship in Israel (1 Kgs 12:25-33). Now the Lord assures Ephraim that he becomes spiritually like a mighty man and his heart is filled with joy.

entries.section: 3. Enjoying victory and the restoration of the kingdom:

paragraphs.text: Fourth: He gathers their dispersion and makes them grow in His bosom: "I will whistle for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them: and they shall increase as they have increased" [8]. He is like the beekeeper who whistles to his scattered bees to gather honey from the meadows and gardens. He gathers them to Himself and grants them by blessing to grow and multiply as they had formerly multiplied, meaning that if He cared for them while they were under chastening, under the bondage of Pharaoh, so that they grew as much as they humbled them (Ex 1:7), will He not rather make them grow and multiply when He redeems them from bondage?!

He fulfills in them His promise to Abraham, the father of the fathers: "for I will make thee a father of a multitude of nations. And I will make thee exceeding fruitful, and I will make nations of thee" (Gen 17:5-6), and as it was said in Isaiah: "A little one shall become a thousand, and a small one a strong nation" (Isa 60:22). And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [If these words were taken literally they would appear difficult, for many of the saints had no children at all, like Elijah and Elisha and John the Baptist, to whom no one attained in virtue and in the knowledge of the holy mysteries (Mt 11:11), and yet he had no children; therefore we must understand that spiritually]. So from one side they have children in the Spirit, like those whom Paul begot in the Gospel (1 Cor 4:15), for whom he travailed until Christ be formed in them (Gal 4:19), or those whom Peter the Apostle calls "obedient children" (1 Pet 1:14), and from another side they have children in the heart, that is, the fruits of the Holy Spirit manifested in us as children who rejoice God's heart!

entries.section: 3. Enjoying victory and the restoration of the kingdom:

paragraphs.text: Fifth: As He brings them back to Himself to grow and bear fruit by the Holy Spirit, He again sows them among the peoples as living seed buried in the earth to bring forth much fruit, for He says: "And I will sow them among the people: and they shall remember me in far countries; and they shall live with their children, and turn again. And I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Assyria; and I will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon; and place shall not be found for them. And he shall pass through the sea of affliction, and shall smite the depths in the sea, and all the deeps of the river shall dry up: and the pride of Assyria shall be brought down, and the sceptre of Egypt shall depart away. And I will strengthen them in the LORD; and they shall walk in his name, saith the LORD" [9-12].

What a living and joyful picture of God's work in them: after He gathers them from the captivity of sin and brings them back to Himself, He casts them as living seed among the peoples to witness to salvation in far lands and to have spiritual sons in the Lord. But they do not walk in the spirit of the world; rather their hearts return from the symbolic land of Egypt, that is, the love of the world, and the Lord gathers them from Assyria, that is, from the spirit of pride, and brings them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon; and lest this be understood materially He said: "and place shall not be found for them," for they are in a state of continual migration and constant going forth from strength to strength and from glory to glory, their hearts raised in the heavenly places, with no place on earth!

St. Didymus the Blind comments on this statement as a declaration of the spiritual migration of the believer: [who passes from vice to virtue. This is truly a change of country, a change from sin to righteousness, from evil to godliness... and he goes from virtue to virtue (Ps 83:8), and passes from the shadow of the Law, where is the letter that kills, to reach the Spirit that gives life (2 Cor 3:6)]... St. Didymus also sees that the migration to the spiritual Lebanon is a migration to the state of deification, that is, the enjoyment of the attributes of the Lord Jesus, where the soul enters into the glorious holy Church, "not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing" (Eph 5:27), of which it is said: "the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon" (Song 4:11).

entries.section: 3. Enjoying victory and the restoration of the kingdom:

paragraphs.text: As He brings them into the new Lebanon, that is, the holy life of the Church, He passes with them through the sea of affliction, like the living fish that hides in the waters with all their disturbances and the sea with all its waves without losing its life... They enter into affliction in this world but the depths of the world cannot swallow them nor the deeps of the river draw them away! Rather they come out of every affliction with greater strength, declaring the Kingdom of God within them; therefore He ends His speech about the blessings of this age by saying: "And I will strengthen them in the LORD; and they shall walk in his name, saith the LORD" [12].

entries.section: 1. A lament over those who reject:

paragraphs.text: 1 Open thy doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour thy cedars. 2 Howl, O cypress; for the cedar is fallen; because the mighty are ruined: howl, O ye oaks of Bashan; for the impenetrable forest is come down. 3 There is a voice of the howling of the shepherds; for their glory is ruined: a voice of the roaring of young lions; for the pride of Jordan is ruined.

Israel's rejection of the Lord Christ turned it into total ruin, so the prophet laments it, saying: "Open thy doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour thy cedars. Howl, O cypress; for the cedar is fallen; because the mighty are struck: howl, O ye oaks of Bashan; for the impenetrable forest is come down. There is a voice of the howling of the shepherds; for their glory is ruined: a voice of the roaring of young lions; for the pride of Jordan is ruined" [1-3].
And it is noticed in this lament:

First: that the ruin carries extended and comprehensive dimensions, striking Lebanon and Bashan and the Jordan, as if the Jews' rejection of the Lord Christ brought them down under an extended, almost collective blow, for they cried out, "His blood be on us, and on our children." And the comprehensiveness does not stop at places but includes the kinds of trees: the cedar that is burned with fire and the cypress that howls and also the oak, as the trees of the forest fall, etc...
Second: He calls nature to mourn for the man who denied his Creator and rejected His work of salvation and even betrayed Him for thirty pieces of silver.

Third: What he mentions here was fulfilled literally, for it was the custom of enemies, when they seized a fertile land like the Promised Land, to cut down its trees to profit from their wood or to burn them with fire with the intent of destruction and ruin.

Fourth: From the symbolic side, what does Lebanon signify in his saying: "Open thy doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour thy cedars"? The enemies entered Lebanon through its doors, that is, through the entrances of the mountains that lead to the city, in order to destroy its cedars of which it is proud. We saw Lebanon spiritually in the previous chapter as signifying the migration to the holy Church to bear in us the sweet fragrance of Christ, for it is said: "the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon" (Song 4:11). And as Lebanon signifies the fruitful Church that bears the attributes of the Lord and His fragrance and the fruit of His Holy Spirit, it also, as St. Didymus the Blind says, signifies on the other side paganism (apostasy from the faith) and arrogance, for he says: [Indeed when the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs calls the Church of the victorious He says to her: Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse (Song 4:8)... she comes to Him who calls her from ignorance and unbelief to holy knowledge and perfect faith].

Fifth: What befalls the cedar and the cypress and the oak and the forest signifies the Jewish groups that rejected the Messiah the Savior, and also signifies the sins that lie hidden in the soul which drive man to be deprived of enjoying salvation. St. Didymus the Blind sees in the haughty cedar an allusion to the company of the proud or to the demon of pride, for he says: [It is written in Isaiah against these barren, fruitless trees: "For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low" (Isa 2:12), and a little after: "And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan" (Zech 2:13). These wild trees grow upon pride... They will be consumed by the fire, the corrupt, the diligent, as Isaiah himself says: "and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one" (Isa 10:34)]. St. Didymus also sees that if the cedar signifies the pride of the great, then the cypress, which is a small tree, signifies those subject to them; if the cedar signifies those who are wise and prudent in their own eyes, then the cypress signifies those who walk in their current. Therefore when fire devours the cedar the cypress mourns the fall of the mighty who are their lords in their eyes.

As for the oak of Bashan, it signifies the dense forests full of leafy trees but without fruit; they represent the hypocrites who have the appearance of religion and deny its power. And the forest is the trees found in the wildernesses and also without fruit!

Sixth: The prophet turned in his speech to the shepherds who left their pastoral work and began to howl because the young lions roar to devour and there is none to deliver, and because the Jordan with its pride, because of the dense forests and the trees in which the wild beasts hide, has been ruined.

This is the broad outline of the lament that the prophet laid upon every soul that rejects the work of salvation in it: its doors open before the enemy so that it loses all its trees, nature grieves over it, and eternal spiritual destruction comes upon it.

entries.section: 2. Their destroying themselves:

paragraphs.text: 4 Thus saith the LORD my God; "Feed the flock of the slaughter; 5 Whose possessors slay them, and hold themselves not guilty: and they that sell them say, Blessed be the LORD; for I am rich: and their own shepherds pity them not. 6 For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land, saith the LORD: but, lo, I will deliver the men every one into his neighbour's hand, and into the hand of his king: and they shall smite the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them."

"Thus saith the LORD my God; Feed the flock of the slaughter, whose possessors slay them, and hold themselves not guilty: and they that sell them say, Blessed be the LORD; for I am rich: and their own shepherds pity them not" [4-5].

Since they rejected the Messiah, the sacrificial Lamb, for their own sake, for perdition and destruction, they became, by their rejection of salvation, without price; their owners slay them and it is not counted against them as sin since they deserve slaughter; and if their owner sells them he is relieved of them as they were a burden to him, so at the sale he says: Blessed be the LORD, I am rich. Perhaps by this he portrays for us the condition of the Jews after they rejected the Savior, as they were scattered in many lands and were exposed to bitter persecutions, every nation wishing to be rid of them as a burden upon them.

The wonder is that God allows the wicked to have harsh shepherds in order to discipline them, for He says: "their own shepherds pity them not." For shepherds are from God; when He is pleased with His people He says: "And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding" (Jer 3:15), that is, they offer them pastures of knowledge and understanding or pastures of divine wisdom that come from God (Eph 4:11; 1 Cor 12:28); but when He is angry with His people He leaves them to themselves and they feed in the pastures of "the wisdom of this world" (1 Cor 2:6), and He delivers them to the pasture of "a reprobate mind" (Rom 1:28), and the pasture of "vile affections" (Rom 1:26).

Good shepherds lead the flock into the bosom of God so that they enjoy security, but the wicked drive them outside God so that they perish; therefore the Psalmist says: "For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish: thou destroyest all them that go a whoring from thee. But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may declare all thy works" (Ps 73:27).

entries.section: 2. Their destroying themselves:

paragraphs.text: They rejected the Good Shepherd, the Messiah the Savior, so they were deprived even of good shepherds, and the Lord delivered them to shepherds who have no pity on the flock... since He Himself no longer has pity on them, for He says: "For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land, saith the LORD: but, lo, I will deliver the men every one into his neighbour's hand, and into the hand of his king: and they shall smite the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them" [6]. He called them "the inhabitants of the land" because they rejected the heavenly Messiah, who came to raise them from earth to heaven, so they remained in their hearts on the earth and were counted "inhabitants of the land" and even bore in them the nature of the earth. This earthly nature bears neither heavenly love nor largeness of heart, but every man delivers his brother to affliction and injustice for his destruction.

entries.section: 3. Their deprivation of divine grace:

paragraphs.text: 7 And I fed the flock of slaughter; but they are the most downtrodden of the flock. And I took unto me two staves; the one I called Grace, and the other I called Bands; and I fed the flock. 8 Three shepherds also I cut off in one month; and my soul was distressed with them, and their soul also hated me. 9 Then said I, I will not feed you: that that dieth, let it die; and that that is to be cut off, let it be cut off; and let the rest eat every one the flesh of another. 10 And I took my staff, even Grace, and cut it asunder, that I might break my covenant which I had made with all the tribes. 11 And it was broken in that day: and so the most downtrodden of the flock that waited upon me knew that it was the word of the LORD.

It was the custom in ancient times for the shepherd to hold two staves, with one of which he struck any wild beast that attacked the flock and with the other he led the flock so that it would not stray from the way, but the Lord appears here holding two staves, which are: grace or beauty, and bands or union; so He leads us by His grace in His green heavenly pastures that we may lack nothing, and leads us by union to bind us all together in Him by the spirit of divine love.
St. Didymus the Blind sees that God by these two staves leads the Jews as He leads the Gentiles as His rational flock, and the two staves also signify His work as Savior and as King.

entries.section: 3. Their deprivation of divine grace:

paragraphs.text: In any case, by the Jews' rejection of the Messiah the King, the Lord broke the staff of Grace, so they were deprived of divine help and lost His blessings because they broke His covenant. Thus they lost His compassionate care: "Then said I, I will not feed you: that that dieth, let it die; and that that is to be cut off, let it be cut off; and let the rest eat every one the flesh of another" [9], not out of contempt for the sheep but because of His sanctification of human freedom, so He left them to themselves, by themselves, apart from His grace.

He says: "Three shepherds also I cut off in one month; and my soul was distressed with them, and their soul also hated me" [8]. Who are these three shepherds whom the Lord destroyed and whom the Jews lost? St. Jerome sees that these three are Moses, Aaron and Miriam, who died shortly before the people entered the Promised Land. Perhaps he means that by their rejection of the Lord Christ they lost His threefold care as priest and king and giver of prophecy, so they were deprived of His atoning intercession (His priesthood) and of His kingship as a leader who conquers and brings them into victory, and of the giver of prophecy who reveals to them the mysteries of the life to come. In ancient times the king was not the priest and not the seer or prophet, but in Christ these three were gathered on a surpassing and unique level.

entries.section: 4. Their betrayal of the Messiah:

paragraphs.text: 12 And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my wages; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver. 13 And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD. 14 Then I cut asunder mine other staff, even Bands, that I might break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

God did not want to present this dark picture of what the people of the circumcision came to because of their rejection of the Messiah without revealing the picture of this rejection in the act of betrayal that Judas committed against his Lord for thirty pieces of silver, which represents the betrayal of the whole people, for they valued Him at the price of a slave who deserves death.

"And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my wages; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter in the house of the LORD" [12-13].

First: What is the silver that was offered as the price of betraying the Lord? St. Didymus the Blind says: [Let us take the wages and the silver from the spiritual side. Silver often signifies divine knowledge and the divine word, as in the saying: "The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times" (Ps 12:6), and it is said in Proverbs: "The tongue of the just is as choice silver" (Prov 10:2). Here the word "tongue" means "speech." But not every word of "silver" is taken in a good sense, for the Lord says of the erring priests of the Jews: "Thy silver is become dross" (Isa 1:22). Here He does not accuse the silver in itself but their deceptive speech, so the Lord says of those who utter this speech: "Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the LORD hath rejected them" (Jer 6:3), since He rejected the deceivers of zeal and the breakers of the commandments. In the same way we understand what is said in Proverbs that silver given to deceit must be taken as a piece of pottery (Prov 26:23); this is the speech of those who care only for earthly things (earthen pottery), of whom it was said by Isaiah: "their voice comes from the earth" (Isa 8:19). So there are kinds of silver, for since the people of the circumcision decided on a wage for Him who suffered for them of thirty pieces of silver (Mt 20:28; Mk 10:5; Jn 10:15)... they paid adulterated silver... presenting deceitful words. And in Christianity also there are people whose beliefs are wrong, "those who walk in craftiness and adulterate the word of God" (2 Cor 4:2), understanding the word of God according to their passions. Of these we must beware and count their talk adulterated silver].
It is as though the Jews and the heretics, as they present adulterated and deceitful words, sell the Lord for adulterated silver!

Second: They counted Him a slave, so they paid the price, thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (Ex 21:32). Perhaps the number 30 symbolizes the defilement of the five senses, for if the number 6 signifies deficiency, then the number 5 (the senses) multiplied by 6 yields 30. It is as though the price of betraying the Lord Christ is the defilement of our senses for the benefit of His enemy the devil instead of sanctifying them to Him.

Third: What does he mean by the potter into whose house the silver was cast in the house of the Lord? St. Didymus the Blind sees that the adulterated silver that was paid as a price for the Lord Christ for betraying Him meets in the house of Holy Scripture, which is the house of the potter, where is the testing fire, which exposes their deceptions and reveals their contradiction with the prophecies concerning the Lord.

Fourth: As the potter deals with dust and clay with fire, the casting of silver into the potter's house declares the nature of their earthly, dusty heart; it is not fitting that it be put in palaces or treasuries but in the dust.

Fifth: With this price a field was bought, called "the field of blood," used for the burial of strangers (Mt 27:7), an allusion to the acceptance of the Gentiles, where we are buried with Christ by the price of His blood that we may rise with Him. St. Jerome says: [The price of Christ is the place of our burial, and the field has been called "the field of blood"; it is the field of the blood of the Jews but it is the place of our burial, because we are strangers and foreigners and have no place of rest. He was crucified and died and we were buried with Him].

entries.section: 4. Their betrayal of the Messiah:

paragraphs.text: Sixth: He ends His speech about the rejection of the Messiah and their betrayal of Him by saying: "Then I cut asunder mine other staff, even Bands (union), that I might break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel" [14]. St. Didymus the Blind sees that the two staves will come together and be united as one staff, as it is written in (Ezek 37), when the Jews return at the end of the ages and accept the Lord Christ, and so become with Judah (the Church of the New Covenant) one by entering the faith.

entries.section: 5. Their acceptance of the Antichrist:

paragraphs.text: 15 And the LORD said unto me, Take unto thee yet the instruments of a foolish shepherd. 16 For, lo, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, which shall not visit those that be cut off, neither shall seek that which is driven away, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed that which standeth still: but he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their hoofs in pieces. 17 Woe to the worthless shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened.

entries.section: 5. Their acceptance of the Antichrist:

paragraphs.text: Since they rejected the Lord Christ, the Good Shepherd, they were deprived of divine grace and of unity together in the Lord by the breaking of the two staves and accepted the false shepherding of the Antichrist, for He says: "Take unto thee yet the instruments of a foolish shepherd, for, lo, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, which shall not visit those that be cut off, neither shall seek that which is driven away, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed that which standeth still: but he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their hoofs in pieces" [16].

St. Didymus the Blind comments on this statement, saying: [God, who leaves them in their shame, has raised up for them a foolish shepherd without experience in shepherding, who destroys those who chose him as their shepherd. He does not care for the one who strayed and became alone, far from the flock, to bring him back, who separated by his straying. He does not preserve anything, nor seek those who were scattered, nor care for the wounded, nor lead the healthy. His aim is evil and not good; he runs after his own advantage and his greed, so he devours the flesh and tears off the hoofs of those under his care. He is not like the shepherds whom God gives, saying: "And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding" (Jer 3:15). For can they be anything but good shepherds, those whose head is He who gives His life for the sheep as the Good Shepherd (Jn 10:15)...? For it was said: "And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away" (1 Pet 5:4). Those who shepherd the sheep thus do not lord it over those who are their charge (1 Pet 5:3), while those who eat the flesh of the sheep seek their own pleasure, thinking that they find glory in the shame of their deeds. They eat without discrimination, so their god is their belly (Phil 3:19) and they are slaves to it, not slaves of Christ Jesus. Of these the Apostle writes: "For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" (Rom 16:18)].

What does he mean by tearing off the nails? Good shepherds keep "the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Eph 4:3), but the wicked tear from the flock its nails, as they are torn from the fingers, that is, they cause it to lose its unity.

entries.section: 5. Their acceptance of the Antichrist:

paragraphs.text: This is the fruit of the people's evil: the Lord leaves it to a foolish shepherd who scatters it as he scatters himself, for He says: "Woe to the worthless shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened" [17]. And as St. Didymus the Blind says concerning this sword which shatters the arm of the foolish shepherd and his right eye: [The word of God threatens especially the bad shepherds... So the Lord says in Isaiah: "If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: but if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword" (Isa 1:19-20), and He speaks in Jeremiah of the avenging sword: "I will stretch out my hand upon the inhabitants of the land" (Jer 6:12) so that they perish... The avenging sword is upon the arm (of the foolish shepherd) and his eye, that is, it touches the two senses of work and contemplation, so his arm is dried up as it becomes a dead member, and his right eye is struck with blindness...].

St. Didymus sees in this prophecy a reference to the Antichrist, who has a strong arm through the signs he performs (2 Thess 2:9), while his right eye signifies his intellectual deceptions, as he claims perfect knowledge though he is a liar (1 Tim 6:20), and Elymas the sorcerer bore a symbol of him, who deceived by his sorcerous works and his lies, so his works were nullified and he was struck with blindness so that he did not see the sun (Acts 13:10).

entries.section: 1. The nations' revolt against Jerusalem:

paragraphs.text: 1 The burden of the word of the LORD for Israel, saith the LORD, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him. 2 "Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling unto all the people round about, when they shall be in the siege both against Judah and against Jerusalem. 3 And in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it."

When the soul receives its Christ within it, the new Jerusalem becomes a member of the house of Judah, and in proportion to the graces it receives it meets resistance from the enemy (the nations), by God's permission, so that the evil of the wicked one may fill its cup and the Lord, the Giver of victory, may be revealed in His children. Through the enemy's harassment of God's children, the others become a cup of trembling to the first, and a burdensome stone to him, and a fire that burns him, as the prophet says: "Saith the LORD, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him, Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling unto all the people round about, when they shall be in the siege both against Judah and against Jerusalem. And in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it" [1-3].

The cup of trembling often signifies the wrath of God, when a man drinks it and loses consciousness and becomes like one in a state of reeling without balance, so that no one, not even one of his sons or daughters, is able to lead him or take him by the hand. This is as it is written in Isaiah: "Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out. There is none to guide her among all the sons whom she hath brought forth; neither is there any that taketh her by the hand of all the sons that she hath brought up" (Isa 51:17-18). And as it was said by Jeremiah: "Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it. And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them" (Jer 25:15).

So when God wishes to give these peoples (as a symbol of the devil) the cup of His wrath to drink, that they may reel, He leaves them to stretch out their hands against Judah, and they fall under the wrath of God, the full measure of their own cup.
Once again God likens His children to the lifted stone, which the wicked carry in order to throw it down and shatter it, but behold, they are cut in pieces, or crushed, beneath it.

entries.section: 2. The salvation of the house of Judah:

paragraphs.text: 4 In that day, saith the LORD, I will smite every horse with astonishment, and his rider with madness: and I will open mine eyes upon the house of Judah, and will smite every horse of the people with blindness. 5 And the governors of Judah shall say in their heart, The inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be my strength in the LORD of hosts their God. 6 In that day will I make the governors of Judah like a lamp of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire among the sheaves; and they shall devour all the people round about, on the right hand and on the left: and Jerusalem shall abide again in her own place, even in Jerusalem. 7 The LORD also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah. 8 In that day shall the LORD defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and he that stumbleth among them at that day shall be as David; and the house of David shall be as God, as the angel of the LORD before them. 9 And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.

"In that day, saith the LORD, I will smite every horse with astonishment, and his rider with madness: and I will open mine eyes upon the house of Judah, and will smite every horse of the people with blindness" [4].

He smites the horse and its rider, who resists God's work in His children. The blow is astonishment, madness and blindness; that is, the enemy loses his peace, his balance and his insight, while the Lord opens His eyes upon the house of Judah, His Church, and becomes her leader and helper, and by Him He strikes the enemy with blindness, so that he is confused in his warfare and loses the battle.

St. Didymus the Blind sees that the horse here is the demon of error, falsehood and cunning, and its riders are those who promote these erroneous teachings, full of deceit; and that the blindness that strikes it is its deprivation of the Sun of Righteousness, who gives light. He also comments on God's opening His eyes upon the house of Judah, saying: [Afterward God opens His eyes upon the house of Judah, which is the church of the living God (1 Tim 3:15), where the Savior, who came from the tribe of Judah, reigns over those who have received wisdom from God, who say: "Judah, thou art he whom thy brethren shall praise: thy hand shall be in the neck of thine enemies; thy father's children shall bow down before thee" (Gen 49:8)... Upon the house of Judah the watchful God opens His eyes, that is, His luminous, watchful powers, and they enjoy enlightenment and grace, and each one prays, saying: "Look upon me and have mercy upon me" (Ps 25:16). This gift is enjoyed by all the righteous, for "the eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry" (Ps 34:15)].

entries.section: 2. The salvation of the house of Judah:

paragraphs.text: Not only is God the mystery of enlightenment to the house of Judah while He strikes the enemy with blindness, but He is also the mystery of strength to His people and the shattering of the devil, His enemy, for "the governors of Judah shall say in their heart, The inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be my strength in the LORD of hosts their God" [5].

entries.section: 2. The salvation of the house of Judah:

paragraphs.text: St. Didymus the Blind sees that if the Messiah is the spiritual King of His Church, then the disciples are the governors of Judah, who receive God as their God, a strength to them in their work of preaching. He gives them a divine, fiery power that burns up the sheaves of straw, for he says: "In that day will I make the governors of Judah like a lamp of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire among the sheaves; and they shall devour all the people round about, on the right hand and on the left: and Jerusalem shall abide again in her own place, even in Jerusalem. The LORD also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah" [6-7].

Although the new Judah has been called the little flock, it carries the fire of the Holy Spirit, which destroys the satanic blows from the right (self-righteousness) and from the left (impurities and lusts), and keeps the believer steadfast like Jerusalem, able to behold peace. St. Didymus the Blind says: [Being spiritually the governors of Judah, it is fitting for them to shatter, with their luminous, fiery speech, the deep fleshly will... It was said by Isaiah: "And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; and shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body" (Isa 10:17-18), meaning that He destroys the corrupt intention as well as the corrupt deeds]. It is as though the fire of the Holy Spirit, who works in the spiritual man, burns the peoples round about, on the right hand and on the left; that is, He burns the evil intentions and deeds of the soul and the body together.
St. Didymus the Blind sees that the right hand and the left here signify extremes, for the Holy Spirit burns in the believer the spirit of stinginess as He burns the spirit of extravagance.

entries.section: 2. The salvation of the house of Judah:

paragraphs.text: It is wonderful that when God works by His fiery Spirit in the house of Judah, He begins with the tents of Judah [7] before saving the houses and palaces, that no one may have cause for boasting. He begins with the dwellers in tents, who are without protection, that they may not boast in their victory that they obtained salvation by their strength and their impregnable fortresses and their palaces and houses.

St. Didymus the Blind speaks of the tents of Judah that the Lord saves, saying: [These tents are the virtue of which it is said in Proverbs: "The tabernacle of the upright shall flourish" (Prov 14:11), and as the psalmist sings concerning the love that these tents inspire in him: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" (Ps 83:1). How should they not be loved, when they are full of those who keep their feasts, for the voices of joy and the works of grace cannot appear in any place other than the tents of the righteous (Ps 41:5; 17:15)?!].

He also sees in the tents of Judah a symbol of the mortal, humbled body that we wear, for when it enjoys God's salvation it puts on incorruption, glory and power, and is changed from a natural body to a spiritual body (1 Cor 15:42-44).

entries.section: 2. The salvation of the house of Judah:
